VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

A. Christian Unity and Its Theological Basis (4:1–6)

B. The Gifts of the Victorious Christ Cultivate the Body’s Maturity (4:7–16)


A. Christian Unity and Its Theological Basis (4:1–6)

In 4:1–6 Paul provides a transition from his description of “the calling” with which his readers “were called” to his practical admonitions for how they should “walk.” The inferential particle οὖν (oun, therefore) reaches back to all of chapters 1–3 (cf. Rom. 12:1), but particularly to the important theme of the church’s unity that Paul has developed there. The newly constituted people of God is not divided along ethnic lines but is “one new human being” (2:15) at peace with itself (2:14) and with its Creator (2:13, 17). This unified church, moreover, proclaims to the inimical powers “in the heavenly places” the beautifully complex wisdom of God (3:10). With the present tenses in 2:21–22, however, Paul has already hinted that there is a tension here. The unity that the church already possesses by means of the death of Christ and the indwelling Spirit is, in some sense, not yet complete: the church is still growing into it (συναρμολογουμένη αὔξει . . . συνοικοδομεῖσθε, synarmologoumenē auxei . . . synoikodomeisthe, being joined together, it grows . . . you are being built together).

In 4:1–6 Paul introduces his practical admonitions on how the church can grow into this ultimate unity. He does this in two parts. The first part offers a general exhortation focused on loving deference to one another (4:1–3), and the second part grounds this general exhortation in the unity of God (“one Spirit . . . one Lord . . . one God and Father”), of God’s people (“one body”), and of the response of God’s people to God (“one hope . . . one faith, one baptism”; 4:1–6).

The two parts have a similar structure. Each part contains a list of items, with the last and longest item in each part bringing its part to a climax. The admonitions to exercise humility, gentleness, patience, and to bear with one another lead to the lengthy exhortation to be “eager to keep the unity of the Spirit by the fastener of peace” (4:3). In the same way, the affirmations of various unities conclude with the lengthy description of “one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all” (4:6).

This final affirmation of God’s unity prepares the way for Paul’s discussion of how he has given “each one” of his readers a measure of grace to use in aiding the church on its way to unity (4:7–16).



Exegesis and Exposition

1Therefore I encourage you, I, the prisoner in the Lord, to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, 2with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with each other in love, 3being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit by the fastener of peace.

4There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called with one hope of your calling. 5There is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, 6one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and ⌜in all⌝.

[4:1] Paul now shifts the discussion to the way of life that should arise from the blessings that God has given to his people. He signals this shift with the phrase παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς (parakalō oun hymas, therefore I encourage you). This movement from theology to ethics, from what God has graciously accomplished for his people to how they should live as a result, is a common feature of the Pauline Letters, and the movement from one to the other is often signaled with οὖν (oun, therefore; 1 Thess. 5:5–6; 2 Thess. 2:15; Gal. 5:1; Phil. 2:1; Rom. 6:12; Col. 3:5–6; Eph. 6:14).[1] Twice Paul uses the precise phrase he employs here, παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς, to make this link (1 Cor. 4:15–16; Rom. 12:1).[2]

By his use of the term παρακαλῶ, Paul also signals that the ethical advice to follow in 4:1–6:20 is given in the context of friendship. This becomes clear from the definition he gives to the term in a letter to his friend and coworker Philemon, written at virtually the same time as Ephesians: “For this reason, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do your duty, yet I would rather appeal [παρακαλῶ] to you on the basis of love—and I, Paul, do this as an old man, and now also as a prisoner of Christ Jesus. I am appealing [παρακαλῶ] to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I have become during my imprisonment” (Philem. 8–10 NRSV).[3] The advice Paul gives in Eph. 4:1–6:20, like the advice he gives to Philemon concerning Onesimus, is issued to friends. He does not know all of his audience personally, but he knows their situation well enough to be thankful for their faith in the Lord Jesus and love for all the saints (1:15).[4] In his advice to them about how to “walk,” he will remind them of what he assumes they have already learned for the purpose of encouraging them to love each other in concrete ways (4:20–24).[5]

Paul’s reference to himself as “the prisoner in the Lord” recalls the similar self-description in 3:1, as well as the reference to his suffering for them in 3:13, and gives a certain gravitas to the instructions that follow. Paul so sincerely holds the convictions out of which this ethical advice flows that he is willing to suffer the physical pain and social stigma of imprisonment to be faithful to them (cf. the comments on 3:1 and 6:20).

He appeals to his readers to περιπατῆσαι (peripatēsai, walk) in a way that is worthy of the calling God has given them. He last used the term περιπατέω in 2:1–10, to bracket his description of how God has brought his readers from an existence under the power of the world, the devil, and the flesh to an existence as God’s graciously restored creatures. Although they once “walked” in transgressions and sins (2:2), they now must “walk” in the good works God has intended for them from the first (2:10). In the second half of the letter, Paul will show in concrete terms how his readers’ new way of “walking” should look (4:17; 5:2, 8, 15).

With the phrase ἀξίως . . . τῆς κλήσεως ἧς ἐκλήθητε (axiōs . . . tēs klēseōs hēs eklēthēte, worthily . . . of the calling with which you were called), Paul refers to his readers’ conversion, the point at which they heard and believed the gospel (1:13; cf. Gal. 1:15; 1 Cor. 1:26; 7:18, 20–22, 24). In the Pauline corpus, God’s call comes to people entirely at God’s initiative (Rom. 4:17; 8:30) and as a free gift (Gal. 1:6, 15), unrelated to any prior merit in those whom he calls, no matter their socioeconomic status (1 Cor. 1:26), their ethnicity (Rom. 9:24–26), or their actions (Rom. 9:12; 2 Tim. 1:9).

This call certainly has immediate, present ramifications—it immediately places those who receive it in fellowship with God’s Son, Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 1:9)—but, as the other two references to it in Ephesians emphasize (1:18, 4:4), it is oriented primarily toward the believer’s future “hope.” It is a call to have a share in the future establishment of God’s kingdom at the time of Jesus’s coming (1 Thess. 2:12; 5:23–24; 2 Thess. 2:14; Eph. 1:18; 4:4; cf. Phil. 3:14; 1 Tim. 6:12).

In 1 Thessalonians, Paul’s understanding of the call of God implies that between the time of conversion, when the call first comes, and the time of Jesus’s parousia, when it is fulfilled, believers should “walk . . . worthily [περιπατεῖν . . . ἀξιως, peripatein axiōs] of the God who has called” them (1 Thess. 2:12; 5:23–24). Here in Eph. 4:1, Paul has the same idea in mind. God has called Paul’s readers to be part of his people not because of anything they have done (cf. 2:8–9) or because of the social group to which they belong (cf. 2:11–13), but as a free gift. They now need to live in a way that is consistent with this past, free call of God and in light of the “hope” to which they have been called (1:18; 4:4; cf. 2 Thess. 1:11; Gal. 5:13; 1 Cor. 7:15; Col. 3:15; 2 Tim. 1:9).

[4:2–3] Paul next uses four expressions to describe in general terms how he wants his readers to live out the calling they have received from God. The Greek can be construed in various ways, but the element of symmetry in the four expressions and the lack of any main verb for the two participles hints that it is best to see all four phrases as adverbial qualifiers of the infinitive περιπατῆσαι (peripatēsai, to walk; v. 1). The first two expressions are prepositional phrases beginning with μετά (meta, with), and the last two expressions begin with nominative participles (ἀνεχόμενοι, anechomenoi, bearing with; σπουδάζοντες, spoudazontes, being eager). The nominative case is unusual, and most modern commentators think it signals an imperatival use of the participle (e.g., Best 1998: 364; O’Brien 1999: 278; Hoehner 2002: 510; cf. BDF §468.2), but the two participles probably simply agree with the logical subject of περιπατῆσαι, which is now understood in an imperatival sense (Abbott 1897: 106; Wallace 1996: 652). As Robinson (1904: 175) comments, “St Paul is fond of passing suddenly to the nominative of a participle,” to which we might add, especially in Colossians and Ephesians (Col. 1:10, 23; 2:2, 7; Eph. 3:17). We should understand the four expressions, then, as adverbial modifiers of περιπατῆσαι: they tell Paul’s readers how they should walk in a manner worthy of their calling.

First, they should do this μετὰ πάσης ταπεινοφροσύνης καὶ πραΰτητος (meta pasēs tapeinophrosynēs kai praytētos, with all humility and gentleness). The term ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosynē, humility) is uncommon in first-century Greek, but when it occurs, it has decidedly negative connotations.[6] Josephus says that the Roman emperor Galba was accused of ταπεινοφροσύνη by the praetorian guard, to whom he had refused the usual celebratory pay bonus on his accession (J.W. 4.494). This was viewed as “low” or “base,” and it turned out to be fatal (Cary 1957: 596–99). Ταπεινοφροσύνη was the opposite of “a noble spirit” (γενναῖος, gennaios; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.24.54, 56, 58; cf. 1.9.10]), and by the late second century the cultivation of ταπεινοφροσύνη as a virtue among Christians became the object of ridicule (Origen, Cels. 6.15).

The Christian understanding of ταπεινοφροσύνη as a positive quality to be cultivated came from the Jewish Scriptures. There, to be humble (ταπεινοφρονέω, tapeinophroneō) is the opposite of having an exalted view of oneself (Ps. 130:2 LXX [131:2 MT, Eng.]),[7] and the “lowly” (ταπεινοί, tapeinoi) are those who have no resources of their own and so need to lean on the Lord for help (Isa. 11:4; 14:32; 49:13; cf. Luke 1:52). The Lord does not despise a “humbled heart” (καρδίαν . . . τεταπεινωμένην, kardian . . . tetapeinōmenēn; Ps. 50:19 LXX [51:19 MT; 51:17 Eng.]). Paul, then, also uses the term positively. In Phil. 2:3 it stands opposite “selfish ambition” (ἐριθεία, eritheia) and “conceit” (κενοδοξία, kenodoxia) and is aligned with “considering others better than yourselves” (BDAG 989–90; cf. 392, 538).

The meaning of the term here in Eph. 4:2 is perhaps best understood from its association with πραΰτη (praytēs), which is “the quality of not being overly impressed by a sense of one’s self-importance” (BDAG 861). Πραΰτης refers to “gentleness” (2 Cor. 10:1) and even “politeness,” especially in circumstances where it takes an effort to be gentle and polite (Sir. 4:8; Gal. 6:1; Titus 3:2; 1 Pet. 3:16). The two terms together, then, refer to an attitude that both recognizes one’s true position before God (a suppliant in need of his help) and is willing to be kind and gracious to others even when circumstances might excuse one from showing these qualities (cf. Col. 3:12–13).

Second, Paul urges his readers to walk μετὰ μακροθυμίας (meta makrothymias, with patience).[8] Μακροθυμία refers to a persistence in one’s convictions, even when circumstances make this difficult (2 Cor. 6:6; 2 Tim. 3:10; 4:2; James 5:10). It is linked with faithfulness in the Pauline corpus (Gal. 5:22; 2 Tim. 3:10; cf. Heb. 6:12). Sandwiched as it is here between references to humility and gentleness on one hand and bearing with others on the other hand, it clearly connotes “being able to bear up under provocation” (BDAG 612).

Third, Paul says that his readers should walk in a way worthy of their calling ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων ἐν ἀγάπῃ (anechomenoi allēlōn en agapē, bearing with each other in love). The verb ἀνέχω (anechō) means to put up with something annoying (2 Cor. 11:1, 4, 19–20; cf. 2 Tim. 4:3) or harmful (2 Thess. 1:4; 1 Cor. 4:12). It is possible to “put up” with people that one nevertheless resents and dislikes, but the phrase “in love” shows that this grudging tolerance is not what Paul has in mind (Schlier 1957: 183). The idea is similar to Col. 3:13: they should bear with and forgive each other “even if one has a just complaint against another.”

Fourth, Paul’s readers should walk σπουδάζοντες τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος (spoudazontes tērein tēn henotēta tou pneumatos, being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit). This final adverbial phrase is climactic. It is the goal toward which the other three phrases have been moving and a bridge to the next paragraph (vv. 4–6). Already the qualities of humility, gentleness, and patience (v. 2a) alerted Paul’s readers that his concern lay with their relationships with others. His next phrase has told them that his concern lies even more specifically with their relationships with one another as people in the church (v. 2b). Now he becomes still more specific: they are to maintain energetically the unity that the Spirit has given them despite their differences with one another (2:18, 22). In addition, Paul’s emphasis on “oneness” (ἑνότης, henotēs) points ahead to his main concern in the next three verses, where the term “one” will appear six times within the space of thirty-four words and itself serves as a transition to the next major section (vv. 7–16), where the unity of the church in the midst of a diversity of gifts is the main subject.

Paul seems to envision the unity of the church as something complex. At one level, the church already possesses unity because God’s Spirit has already accomplished it when, in concert with Christ, he tore down the barriers that divided various social groups, giving them peace with each other and peace with God (2:18, 22).[9] At another level, however, the church needs to maintain (τηρεῖν, tērein) unity, and it must live in a way that is zealous to do so (σπουδάζοντες, spoudazontes).[10] At this level, unity is kept “by the συνδέσμῳ [syndesmō] of peace.”[11] The term σύνδεσμος (syndesmos) means a “fastener,” such as something that holds clothing together, a conjunction that attaches clauses to each other, or a ligament that binds bone to muscle (LSJ 1701; cf. BDAG 966). It could also be used metaphorically to refer, for example, to the bond that unites the city (Plato, Resp. 7.520a) or, in Stoicism and Middle Platonism, to the bonds that hold the cosmic body of the universe together (van Kooten 2003: 30–53). For Paul, the metaphor was alive (Col. 2:19), and so here he probably has in mind the imagery of something that fastens things together: peace is the “fastener” that preserves the church’s unity.[12] It must be energetically worked out in practical ways, such as lovingly putting up with each other’s foibles, being polite and gentle under provocation, and being humble.

[4:4] In 4:4–6 Paul utters a series of short statements that begin with the number “one” and focus on the church body, the Spirit, the Christian hope, the Lord, God the Father, the faith, and baptism. The theological importance of these subjects, that they number seven (a significant number in Judaism and early Christianity), the skillful repetition of the three genders for “one” in 4:5, the lack of any main verb, and the lack of any conjunction linking 4:4–6 to the previous paragraph—these features have led many interpreters to see an early Christian creedal formulation here, either in its entirety (Pelikan and Hotchkiss 2003: 34) or in part (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 228–29; Best 1997a: 64–66; 1998: 357–59).[13]

If these features are evidence of an early Christian creed, however, it is likely that Paul has used it with a free hand. He has probably at least added the phrase καθὼς καὶ ἐκλήθητε ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι τῆς κλήσεως ὑμῶν (kathōs kai eklēthēte en mia elpidi tēs klēseōs hymōn, just as you were called with one hope of your calling). The use of καθώς (kathōs, just as) and a verb and noun from the same stem (ἐκλήθητε . . . κλήσεως, eklēthēte . . . klēseōs, you were called . . . with a calling) are both stylistic peculiarities of Ephesians (Lincoln 1990: 229; Best 1997a: 67; 1998: 358). Paul has probably also added the first set of terms, ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα (hen sōma kai hen pneuma, one body and one Spirit), since these have been important in the letter up to this point (σῶμα, sōma, body [1:23]; ἓν σῶμα, hen sōma, one body [2:16]; ἓν πνεῦμα, hen pneuma, one Spirit [2:18]; πνεῦμα, pneuma [1:13, 17; 2:22; 3:5, 16]).[14] Indeed, the number “one” (ἓν, hen) itself seems to echo Paul’s use of the term “unity” (ἑνότης, henotēs) in the immediately preceding clause (v. 3), and this makes the lack of a conjunction joining 4:3 to 4:4 somewhat more natural.

It seems likely, then, that Paul freely composed 4:4–6 as he dictated his letter, perhaps relying to some extent on traditional language from early creedal formulations. Something similar probably happened in 1 Cor. 8:4, where Paul reminded the Corinthians of a truth he and they both knew: “There is no God but one” (οὐδεὶς θεὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς, oudeis theos ei mē heis). This is traditional language (Rom. 3:30; Mark 2:7; 10:18 [par. Luke 18:19]; cf. 1 Tim. 2:5), but it is fully integrated into the surrounding argument. In Eph. 4:4–6 Paul has probably also used some traditional language, but just as in 1 Cor. 8:4, he has so fully integrated it into the context that it is difficult to identify precisely which elements come from the tradition and which elements come from Paul.

The section serves as a theological basis both for the practical admonitions to unity in 4:1–3 and for the emphasis on unity amid diversity in 4:7–16 (cf. Dahl 2000: 418). The sevenfold repetition of the number “one” shows the importance of the unity that Paul appeals to his readers to pursue in 4:1–3, but the diversity within this one God (Spirit, Lord, and Father; on this, see especially Barth 1974: 466–67) and the diverse ways in which his unity finds expression (body, faith, baptism) reveal that God’s unity is nevertheless expressed in the kind of diversity that Paul will describe in 4:7–16.

Structurally, Paul expresses himself here in much the same way as he did in 1 Cor. 12:4–31. There too a description of the diversity within God (“the same Spirit, . . . Lord, . . . [and] God”) and of the correspondingly diverse manifestation of his presence in the church (“gifts, . . . services, . . . and activities”; 12:4–6) lays the groundwork for a discussion of the various gifts given to “the one body” with its “many members” (12:7–31).

Paul begins this new paragraph by affirming that there is ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα (hen sōma kai hen pneuma, one body and one Spirit). This phrase reaches back to 2:13–22, where he had described Christ as both “peace” itself (2:14) and the one who preaches “peace” (2:17). Sandwiched between these two references to peace lies the description of Christ’s creation of “the one new human being” and the “one body” of the church through his death on the cross (2:15–16), a death that tore down the enmity between Jews and Gentiles and reconciled both groups to God. Paul then says that both groups have access to God “in one Spirit” (2:18) and, a few clauses later, that God dwells with his united people “in the Spirit” (2:22). When Paul says that “there is one body and one Spirit,” therefore, he is reminding his readers that they should keep the church fastened together with peace because of what God has done for them both by uniting them together across entrenched social boundaries and by giving them his spiritual presence.

There is “one body” and “one Spirit” in the same way that (καθώς, kathōs) Paul’s readers “have been called” (ἐκλήθητε, eklēthēte) in one hope of their “calling” (κλήσεως, klēseōs). The repetition of the concept of “calling” from 4:1 and the use, as in that verse, of both the noun and the verb that express this concept lend it special emphasis. Here, however, Paul makes the future element of God’s call explicit, just as he did in his first intercessory prayer (1:18): his readers were called ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι (en mia elpidi, in one hope).

Since his prayer, Paul has described this hope more specifically in 2:12. In that section, he said that his readers, prior to their conversion, had no “hope” and were “without God in the world.” They were powerless before Satan’s dominion, their own fallen flesh and mind, and the wrath of God, whom they had disobeyed (2:1–3). They were, moreover, separated from Israel, the people through whom God has worked to rescue human beings from this universal plight (2:11–12). “But now,” because of the blood of Christ, shed on the cross, God has rescued them from this desperate situation by making them part of his people and reconciling them to himself (2:13–18). They now have hope, the same kind of hope that characterized Abraham, who believed that the God who could call things into existence out of nothing could also create a people for himself against all appearances to the contrary (Rom. 4:17–18).

Paul says that his readers were called ἐν (en) this hope. This means that hope accompanied God’s call, as an integral part of it.[15] Like Abraham, their trust in the good news that God has included them in his people and reconciled them to himself is a trust in something they cannot see. It is the conviction that one day what they can now see only with the eyes of their hearts will be concrete, and they will experience for all time “the surpassing wealth of his grace by kindness . . . in Christ Jesus” (2:7).

[4:5] Paul now picks up the pace of his discourse, dropping all conjunctions and qualifying phrases and skillfully varying the terms to which he refers to allow himself to repeat the number “one” in all three genders: εἷς κύριος, μία πίστις, ἓν βάπτισμα (heis kyrios, mia pistis, hen baptisma, one Lord, one faith, one baptism). The repetition shows that his emphasis lies on the numeral itself and not on the three terms to which it is attached. This should caution us against finding a subtle significance in the order of the terms or theological reasons why precisely these three terms and not others were chosen.[16]

His readers have “one Lord,” the same Lord whom Paul serves as a prisoner (4:1) and who is identical with “Messiah Jesus,” the one who stands at the center of God’s purposes for the universe (3:11). He is enthroned at God’s right hand with every other “lordship” (κυριότης, kyriotēs) beneath his feet (1:21). These “lordships” include that of “Nero, the lord of all the universe” (ὁ τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου κύριος Νέρων, ho tou pantos kosmou kyrios Nerōn), as one contemporary inscription described him (SIG 814, line 31, quoted in Foerster, TDNT 3:1056; my trans.; cf. Acts 25:26). Thus the early Christian confession of Jesus as the “one Lord” excluded the Roman emperors and anyone else from legitimate claim to that title (cf. 1 Cor. 8:5–6).

At the same time, the title boldly identified Jesus with the God of the Jewish Scriptures, who is often called ὁ κύριος (ho kyrios, the Lord) in the LXX. Deuteronomy 6:4 in the LXX, for example, reads, “Hear, O Israel, the Lord [κύριος] our God is one Lord [κύριος εἷς, kyrios heis].”

His readers also have “one faith.” This could refer to the body of doctrine that all Christians believe (e.g., Best 1998: 368–69; O’Brien 1999: 283) or to the trust that all Christians place in Christ Jesus (e.g., Eadie 1883: 275; Hoehner 2002: 516–17). Up to this point in the letter, both the verb (πιστεύω, pisteuō, I believe) and the noun (πίστις, pistis, faith) have referred to the trust that Christians place in Christ (1:13, 15, 19; 2:8; 3:12, 17). In 4:13, however, Paul will speak of ἡ ἑνότης τῆς πίστεως (hē henotēs tēs pisteōs, the unity of the faith), clearly echoing 4:3–6 and just as clearly referring to the content of the faith that the apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers of 4:11 have handed on in their teaching. Here too, then, Paul probably means the body of teaching that Christians believe, what he calls in 1:13 “the word of truth, the gospel of . . . salvation” (cf. Gal. 1:23; 1 Cor. 16:13; Rom. 10:8).

His readers have experienced “one baptism.” Most interpreters believe that this refers to the Christian practice of immersion in water (e.g., BDAG 165), although they sometimes allow that a reference to Spirit baptism may lurk in the background (e.g., Best 1998: 369). Yet we should remember that the word βαπτίζω (baptizō) means “I immerse,” not “I immerse in water.”[17] With this in mind, the evidence from the Pauline tradition should make us cautious about assuming that an unqualified reference to baptism, such as we find here, must refer to water baptism. The reference here is rich with echoes of 1 Cor. 12:13: “For we were all also baptized by one Spirit into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free, and we all were irrigated with one Spirit.”[18] If Paul refers to water baptism at all in 1 Cor. 12:13, it takes a distant second place in importance to the notion that God has immersed his people in his Spirit (cf. Mark 1:8; Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16; Acts 1:5; 11:16; Dunn 1998a: 86–88, 95–96).

Similarly, in Gal. 3:26–29 Paul refers to the unity of Christians across boundaries of ethnicity, social class, and gender because of a common faith in Christ, a common faith that he then explains further in terms of baptism into Christ and putting on Christ. The reference to putting on Christ is metaphorical, and so the reference to baptism is best understood as metaphorical also (Dunn 1970: 109–13). Paul thought that water baptism was important enough to practice it (1 Cor. 1:14–16), and he assumed that even Christians he did not know personally had experienced it (Dunn 1998a: 90, citing Rom. 6:3–4; Col. 2:12), but he also gave the ritual itself a place of secondary importance to the faith of the individual in the gospel and the transforming work of the Spirit (1 Cor. 1:13, 17; cf. Gal. 3:2, 5; Eph. 1:13; cf. Dunn 1998a: 95).

Despite all this, it seems likely that in a letter like Ephesians, written to a wide audience, a simple reference to baptism would at least include the Christian ritual (Bruce 1961: 79–80; pace Hoehner 2002: 518). It is perhaps best to think of “one baptism” as a shorthand expression for the whole process of conversion, summarized by reference to the visible ritual. It was “one” because it was distinctively Christian: it was done in the name of Jesus (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5) and symbolized the death (Rom. 6:3–4) and resurrection (Col. 2:12) of the believer with Christ. The ritual was an important symbol of this process but was not nearly as important as the spiritual reality that it signified (cf. Bruce 1961: 79; 1984: 336–37; Dunn 1998a: 93–101; O’Brien 1999: 284).

[4:6] The seventh and final affirmation of unity is also the climax of the series (Lincoln 1990: 240). It focuses on the unity of God as seen in his sovereign fatherhood over “all.” The four occurrences of the term “all” (πάντων . . . πάντων . . . πάντων . . . πᾶσιν, pantōn . . . pantōn . . . pantōn . . . pasin) in this affirmation could be masculine and so refer to people, or they could be neuter and refer to things.

A number of interpreters have thought the terms were masculine and referred to “all” believers (e.g., Alford 1857: 110–11; Eadie 1883: 275–79; Masson 1953: 187; Bruce 1984: 337–38; Schnackenburg 1991: 166–68; Hoehner 2002: 519–20). This reading would be consistent with the idea developed in the letter so far that God is the adoptive Father of believers (1:5) and that they have free access to their Father by means of the “one” Spirit (2:18). The statement that God is “over all and through all and in all,” moreover, coheres nicely with the picture of God ruling over the church through Christ its head (1:20–23) and, by the Spirit, giving access to God (2:18) and indwelling his people (2:22).

Those who see the occurrences of “all” as neuter and interpret the statement of God’s rule over the universe (“all things”), however, have the better argument (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 203–4; Barth 1974: 470–72; O’Brien 1999: 285; Lincoln 1990: 240–41; Darko 2008: 120). They point out that Paul uses similar affirmations elsewhere in his letters, and in those places “all” refers to everything (1 Cor. 8:6; Rom. 11:36; Col. 1:16–17). The notion that the one God and Father ties everything together, moreover, expresses an important theme throughout the letter so far:



He will sum up “all things” (τὰ πάντα, ta panta) in Christ (1:10).

He works “all things” (τὰ πάντα) to accomplish his will (1:11).

He has subjected “all things” (πάντα) to Christ (1:22).

He has created “all things” (τὰ πάντα; 3:9).

He is the Father who names “every” (πᾶσα, pasa) family, whether earthly or heavenly (3:15).

Taken together, these statements seem to spell out what Paul means when he says that God is “over all and through all and in all.” He is “over” all in the sense that he created everything (3:9), named all the tribes of the universe (3:15), and subjected everything to Christ (1:22). He is “through” and “in” all in the sense that he is summing up all things in Christ (1:10) and works all things to accomplish his will (1:11).

As interpreters at least since Jerome (Heine 2002: 170) have sometimes noticed, this understanding of the phrase is consistent with the use of similar expressions within Stoicism of God’s presence everywhere (e.g., Marcus Aurelius, Med. 7.9; cf. 4.23).[19] The expression also resembles affirmations in Hellenistic Judaism that the “one” God is the Creator of “all” (e.g., Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.193) or that God is the “one Father of all” creation (e.g., Philo, Spec. Laws 1.14; cf. Heir 62; cf. Gnilka 1971: 204n2; Dibelius 1956: 24–25). In both the Stoic and the Jewish texts, the term “all” refers to everything that exists, and this broader religious context makes it likely that when Paul speaks in a similar idiom, he uses “all” in the same way.

Paul, then, brings his preface to the second main part of his letter to a climax with the affirmation that the one God is Father of and sovereign over all things. He has created everything and works intentionally through and in all things to accomplish his intended goal for the universe he created.

The church occupies a critical place in this divine plan (1:22–23; 2:11–22; 3:9–10) and so must itself be unified. The uniqueness of God and his plan for the unity of the universe should be reflected in practical ways in the unity of believers with one another.

Summary

Paul introduces the second part of his letter with a brief prologue in two parts. First (4:1–3), he tells his readers that he writes as a friend so committed to what he is about to say that he has been willing to suffer imprisonment for it. He wants to encourage his readers to live in the way their conversion and their hope imply they should live, which means cultivating four qualities in particular: humility that translates into gentleness (even toward difficult people), persistence in their commitment (even when this is difficult), willingness to put up with annoying people (even to love them), and zeal to preserve the Spirit-given unity of the church.

Second (4:4–6), Paul summarizes the theological basis on which this way of life must be built. Christ died to make his church one body out of a diversity of ethnic groups, and the Spirit lives within the church to keep this unity. Christ also died to provide hope to those who had been without hope because they were without God. There is only one Lord, and all Paul’s readers confess him as Lord. There is only one body of truth about this Lord and his significance, and all Paul’s readers believe it. There is only one immersion in the Spirit at conversion (signified by water baptism), and all Paul’s readers have experienced it. There is only one God who created all things and is summing them all up in Christ, and he is the object of the worship of all Paul’s readers.

If Paul’s readers are unified with one another in their willingness to confess these truths, then they should be willing to engage in the practical attitudes and actions that foster the unity of the church for which Christ died.



Additional Note

4:6. In a number of ancient witnesses (e.g., D, F, G, Ψ, 0278, 1739c, most Byzantine manuscripts, the Old Latin and Syriac versons, and Irenaeus), the term ἡμῖν appears immediately after the phrase ἐν πᾶσιν (not before, as Best 1998: 371 says). If this is correct, then the debate over whether the four uses of πᾶς in 4:6 are masculine or neuter can be decided with a reasonable degree of certainty in favor of a masculine reference to the body of believers in the church. If Paul concluded 4:6 with the statement that God is ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμῖν (in us all), then the pronoun ἡμῖν (us) must refer to believers, as it has throughout the letter. The other three occurrences of “all” in 4:6, then, would also refer to believers. On the strength of the geographical diversity of the witnesses that have ἡμῖν, Hoehner (2002: 519n2) accepts this reading and interprets the rest of the verse accordingly.

Most commentators who address the issue, however, have decided to omit ἡμῖν (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 81; Abbott 1897: 109; Robinson 1904: 179; Lincoln 1990: 223; Best 1998: 371; Metzger 1994: 536). Some in the early church, such as Origen (Heine 2002: 168–69) and Marcion (Barth 1974: 471n224), were concerned with the question of whether God was the Father of all people or only of Christians, and a desire to confine God’s fatherhood to believers may have led an early scribe to add the ἡμῖν. The addition also conformed the text to the first-person plural ἡμῶν in 4:7 (Lincoln 1990: 223; cf. Gnilka 1971: 204n3). A later addition of ἡμῖν to the text becomes even more likely when we consider the strength of the witnesses against including it (e.g., 𝔓46, א, A, B, C, P, 082, 6, 33, 81, 104, 1175, 1739*, 1881, 2464, the Coptic tradition, Marcion [according to Epiphanius], Jerome, and Augustine). It is true, as Hoehner (2002: 519n2) says, that this is primarily Alexandrian evidence, but the evidence is so early that it is still quite strong. It is likely, then, that ἡμῖν was not part of the original letter.





VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

A. Christian Unity and Its Theological Basis (4:1–6)

B. The Gifts of the Victorious Christ Cultivate the Body’s Maturity (4:7–16)


B. The Gifts of the Victorious Christ Cultivate the Body’s Maturity (4:7–16)

Paul now moves from the general to the particular and from the given to what still needs attaining. Although there is a sense in which the unity of the body has already been created by the God who is sovereign over all (vv. 4–6), we now learn that there is also a sense in which “each one” in the body must work to attain the body’s unity (vv. 7, 13, 16). This new focus leads Paul to view the body’s unity through the metaphors of architectural completeness (οἰκοδομή, oikodomē, building up; vv. 12, 16) and human maturity (ἀνὴρ τέλειος, anēr teleios, mature man; v. 13), metaphors that recall the language of 2:11–22. In that passage, Christ creates “in himself one new human being” (ἐν αὐτῷ εἰς ἕνα καινὸν ἄνθρωπον, en autō eis hena kainon anthrōpon) through his death (2:15–16) and becomes the most important stone used in the building (οἰκοδομή) where God dwells, a building constructed from both Jews and Gentiles (2:19–22). The building/body is not yet complete, and the effort of each believer is necessary for its completion.

The power for achieving this goal, however, comes not from the believer’s own resources but as a gift from the victorious, ascended Christ. This point is so important that Paul begins the passage with it and supports it with a quotation and exegesis of Ps. 68:18. The very same Christ who has conquered every enemy power in every corner of the universe, whether high or low, is the one who now distributes gifts to each believer “for the building up of the body of Christ” (v. 12).

As with 4:1–6, this paragraph can be divided into two subsections. The first subsection (4:7–10) focuses on the gift-giver, Christ, and on his status as the one who has conquered the forces of evil. The second subsection (4:11–16) is one long sentence. It shifts the emphasis slightly from the gifts given to each person in the body to the gifts of five groups of people to the body of Christ so that they might in turn equip the “saints” for the work of ministry (4:11–12). With mention of the “work” of the “saints,” however, the emphasis quickly moves back to the contribution that “all” make to the body’s maturity (v. 13). This body of Christ, we now learn, is growing and maturing away from infancy (with its tendency to be swayed by various kinds of false teaching) toward full adulthood, and every “connection” in the body assists this growth by his or her loving witness to the truth of the gospel (vv. 14–16).



Exegesis and Exposition

7But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. 8Therefore it says, “Ascending to the height, he captured captivity; ⌜he gave⌝ gifts to human beings.” 9And what does “he ascended” mean except that he also descended ⌜ ⌝ into the lower regions ⌜ ⌝ of the earth. 10The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended far above all the heavens so that he might fill all things.

11And he himself gave ⌜some⌝ to be apostles, ⌜others⌝ to be prophets, ⌜others⌝ to be evangelists, ⌜and others⌝ to be pastors and teachers 12for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, 13until we all arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at a mature man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ, 14that we might no longer be infants, wave-tossed and blown around by every wind of teaching, by human trickery, by cunning, in the service of the system of error, 15but by speaking the truth in love, we might grow up to him in every respect, who is the head, Christ, 16from whom all the body, being joined and held together through every assisting connection according to the activity in the measure of each single part, produces the growth of the body for the purpose of building itself up in love.

[4:7] Paul makes a skillful transition to the new section by beginning his first sentence with ἑνὶ δὲ ἑκάστῳ ἡμῶν (heni de hekastō hēmōn, but to each one of us). The first term, ἑνί (heni, one), links the new passage to the theme of unity that has dominated the previous paragraph (4:1–6), and the δέ (de, but) alerts the reader that Paul is about to change directions slightly: he will now focus on the role of individuals in attaining the unity he has just summarized in 4:1–6.

Paul begins by saying that ἐδόθη ἡ χάρις (edothē hē charis, grace has been given) to each believer κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ (kata to metron tēs dōreas tou Christou, according to the measure of the gift of Christ). The combination of the terms χάρις (charis, grace), δίδωμι (didōmi, give), and δωρεά (dōrea, gift) last occurred in Paul’s digression on his personal role in God’s purposes as a herald of the gospel to the Gentiles (3:2, 7–9). He called this role “the grace [χάρις, charis] that God gave [δίδωμι] me” (3:2), said that he received it “according to the gift [δωρεά] of God’s grace [χάρις] given [δίδωμι] to me according to the effect of his power” (3:7), and claimed that “this grace [χάρις] was given [δίδωμι] . . . to me” (3:8). Paul’s particular role may be historically unique, but now we learn that just as God has graciously given Paul his role (3:2, 7, 8) and the power to carry it out (3:7), so also a role in the edification of the church is given “to each one of us” (cf. 1 Cor. 12:7, 11; Rom. 12:3; 1 Pet. 4:10).[1]

A few scholars have argued that “us” here refers not to every believer but to “the apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers” of verse 11. Merklein (1973: 58–62), for example, thinks that 4:7–16 comes from a time after Paul when the church’s unity and doctrinal purity were at risk. He says Ephesians was written by a follower of Paul who sanctioned certain ecclesiastical offices to guard the church’s unity and doctrinal purity. The offices of verse 11, then, are the “gifts” that Christ “gave” to the church in verses 7–8, and the “us” refers to Paul, his fellow apostles and prophets, and by implication, to the ecclesiastical authorities of the author’s own day who carry on the tradition handed down by the first generation of authorities.[2]

As most commentators recognize, however, this is not a plausible reading of the shift to the first-person plural. So far, the author has used the first-person plural in the letter to include himself with his readers (1:3–12, 14, 17, 19; 2:3–5, 7, 14, 18; 3:12, 20), and it is unlikely that he would expect them suddenly to understand his use of it here in an exclusive sense (Schnackenburg 1991: 175).

Grace is therefore given to each believer, and it is given κατὰ τὸ μέτρον τῆς δωρεᾶς τοῦ Χριστοῦ (kata to metron tēs dōreas tou Christou, according to the measure of the gift of Christ). The expression κατὰ τὸ μέτρον means “according to the due measure, proportion, or limit” (cf. LSJ 1123; 1 Kings 7:48 LXX [7:11 MT, Eng.]; 2 Cor. 10:13). The phrase τῆς δωρεᾶς describes what is measured, and the phrase τοῦ Χριστοῦ explains who measures it: Christ gives “grace” to each believer, and he does so in proportions appropriate to each gift. Just as with 3:2, 7, and 8, the term χάρις carries with it the connotation not only of an assignment given by God but also of the gift of “the powers and capabilities requisite” to complete the assignment (BDAG 1080). Just as in Paul’s own experience of God’s grace (3:7–8), then, Christ measures out to each believer the right amount of power necessary to accomplish the task that the gift requires (cf. v. 16; Rom. 12:6; Pokorný 1992: 169).

[4:8] Paul next introduces a quotation to support his claim that Christ gives to each believer both gifts and the necessary power to employ Christ’s gifts. Paul’s introductory phrase, διὸ λέγει (dio legei, therefore it says), is slightly odd. It appears only here, in 5:14, and in James 4:6 in the NT, and contrary to Paul’s custom with similar introductory phrases, it does not identify the source of his quotation.[3] Although the quotation itself resembles Ps. 68:18 (68:19 MT; 67:19 LXX), it differs from that text in such important ways that some scholars think Paul is not quoting Scripture at all (cf. 5:14).

A table with a literal translation of the relevant texts is perhaps the easiest way to show where the problem lies:

Psalm 68:19 MT Psalm 67:19 LXX Ephesians 4:8



* * *





You ascended (עָלִיתָ, ʿālîtā) to the height; you captured (שָׁבִיתָ, šābîtā) captivity; you received (לָקַתְתָּ, lāqaḥtā) gifts among humanity (בָּאָדָם, bāʾādām). You ascended (ἀνέβης, anebēs) to the height; you captured (ᾐχμαλώτευσας, ēchmalōteusas) captivity; you received (ἔλαβες, elabes) gifts among humanity (ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ, en anthrōpō).[4] Ascending (ἀναβάς, anabas) to the height, he captured (ᾐχμαλώτευσεν, ēchmalōteusen) captivity; he gave (ἔδωκεν, edōken) gifts to human beings (τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, tois anthrōpois).



* * *





As the table shows, the MT and LXX are in step with each other, but Paul’s quotation contains three differences from these other texts, listed here in ascending order of importance:

Paul changes the subject of the statement so that it no longer tells God what he has done in the second person but narrates what Christ has done in the third person.

He changes the collective singular noun “humanity” to the plural noun, “human beings.”

He changes the verb “received” to its antonym “gave” and modifies the end of the statement so that instead of God receiving gifts among humanity (singular), Christ gives gifts to human beings (plural).



These changes produce a significant difference in meaning between Ps. 68:18 (Eng.) and Paul’s quotation. In its original form, Ps. 68:18 tells God that after triumphing over his enemies, he has led them in triumphal procession to a mountaintop (probably Zion) and taken booty from them. Paul’s text speaks quite differently of a triumphant Christ distributing gifts to each of his human subjects.

According to a number of scholars, both the similarity of Paul’s text to Ps. 68:18 and its dramatic departures from the original can be explained if Paul (or the author of Ephesians) knew the Jewish interpretive tradition on this text.[5] With remarkable consistency ancient Jewish interpreters took Ps. 68:18 as a reference to Moses’s ascent to heaven to receive the Torah from God. The “you” in the text was not God but Moses; the ascension was not up Mount Zion but to heaven; and “captivity” was not a collective noun referring to prisoners of war but the Torah.

The phrase “you received gifts among humanity,” however, created a problem for this interpretation. If the text speaks of Moses’s receiving the law from God, then the gifts must be equated with the law. But if the gifts are the law, then they should come from God rather than from people, and Moses should receive them in heaven, where God dwells, not on earth “among humanity.”

One strategy for solving this problem takes the phrase as a reference to “the Torah which was bestowed upon Israel as a gift, at no cost” (Midr. Teh. 68.11; Barth 1974: 475–76; W. H. Harris 1996: 77–95).[6] This interpretation assumes that Moses received the law after ascending to heaven in order to give it to God’s people. The targum on Ps. 68:19 MT makes this assumption explicit by substituting “he gave” for “you received” in its paraphrase of the text: “You ascended to the firmament, Prophet Moses; you led captive captivity; you learned the words of Torah; you gave them as gifts to the sons of men” (Tg. of Ps. 68:19, trans. W. H. Harris 1996: 65, my italics).[7]

If we simply substitute “Christ” for Moses and “gifts” for Torah, the targum’s rendering of Ps. 68:18 (Eng.) is close to Paul’s quotation. Few scholars would say that the author of Ephesians was familiar with the targum as we now have it, since its present form comes from several centuries after Ephesians was written. Many scholars, however, think the author appealed to an exegetical tradition on Ps. 68:18 that also stands behind the targum.[8] Others think that Paul used the Mosaic interpretation of Ps. 68:18 in a polemical way to draw a contrast between Moses and Christ. Moses gave the people law, but Christ gave them grace (v. 7), and Moses ascended to heaven, but Christ ascended “far above the heavens” (v. 10; Lincoln 1982: 20; 1990: 243; Bruce 1984: 342–43).

A variant of this approach says that Eph. 4:8 is indebted to an early Christian argument against the association of Moses, the Torah, and Pentecost with Ps. 68:18. For Paul, as for the early Jewish Christians before him (cf. Acts 2:33), Christ’s ascension to heaven and subsequent gift of the Spirit at Pentecost had trumped Moses’s ascent to heaven and subsequent mediation of the law to Israel (W. H. Harris 1996: 171–72; cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 177; Moritz 1996a: 74–75; Muddiman 2001: 188–89).

What are we to make of these approaches to Paul’s quotation? Since Paul introduces an otherwise unknown saying with διὸ λέγει in 5:14, it is reasonable to propose that here too he quotes not Scripture directly but a traditional paraphrase of Ps. 68:18. Nevertheless, the balance of the evidence favors the view that Paul himself changed the text of the psalm so that it conformed better to his concerns in 4:7–16. This evidence can be summarized in two points.

First, the targum of Ps. 68:19 is the only unambiguous evidence of a Jewish exegetical tradition that actually replaces the verb “received” with the verb “gave” (cf. Schwindt 2002: 403). The other ancient Jewish comments on this text retain the verb “received” in the quotation and only imply in their interpretive comments that Moses received the Torah in order to “give” it to Israel. The targums on the Psalms in their present form, however, come from the fourth or fifth century after Christ, yet the christological reading of Ps. 68:18 was widespread long before this time (Justin, Dial. 39.4–5; 87.6; Tertullian, Marc. 5.8.18; cf. Schwindt 2002: 407). It seems at least as likely, then, that the targum represents a polemical response to the Christian exegesis of Ps. 68:19 as that it preserves a three- or four-hundred-year-old Jewish exegetical tradition that Paul knew and used.

Second, Paul wrote in Greek to Gentiles in Asia Minor (2:11; 3:1; 4:17), not in Aramaic to Jews, nor even in Greek to Jewish Christians. Yet the targums are in Aramaic, the vernacular of Judea, Syria, and Mesopotamia during the time of early Christianity (Kaufman 1992: 173). Paul could have certainly assumed some knowledge of the Greek rendering of the Scriptures among his readers, but he would not have assumed that they were familiar with an exegetical tradition preserved only in an Aramaic paraphrase of the Hebrew Scriptures. Even if some of his readers had heard of the rendering of Ps. 68:18 now preserved in the targum, moreover, it seems unlikely that they gave the targum the same status as the Greek Scriptures (cf. Best 1998: 379–80).

Paul himself, then, changed the Greek rendering of the text to suit his argument at this point in the letter. This should not surprise us. As Best (1998: 381) points out, when Paul quotes Hab. 2:4 in Gal. 3:11 and Rom. 1:17, he leaves out the possessive pronoun “his” so that Habakkuk’s “the righteous person shall live by his faithfulness” becomes “the righteous person shall live by faith.” Similarly, he quotes Deut. 30:12–14 in Rom. 10:6–8 to draw a contrast between the righteousness that comes by faith and the righteousness that comes by the Mosaic law (cf. Calvin 1965: 176). Deuteronomy 30:12–14 is a description of the ease with which one can obey the law. Paul, however, omits from his quotation any reference to the law, makes the text refer to the universal availability of the righteousness that comes by faith, and contrasts the effortlessness of faith with the impossibility of doing the law. Although in each instance Paul has introduced dramatic changes to the text that he cites, a reasonable case can be made that his overall argument is consistent with the overall argument of the passage out of which his citation comes.

Has Paul also followed this procedure in Eph. 4:7–11? Here too, a good case can be made that although Paul’s changes to the Greek text of Scripture are dramatic, they are consistent with the overall theological direction of Ps. 68.

As the threefold use of the verb δίδωμι (didōmi, give) in the passage (vv. 7, 8, 11) shows, the main theme of 4:7–16 is clearly that Christ gave gifts to the church to support its unity and to protect it against false teaching. The critical change in the wording of Ps. 68:18 from “you received” to “he gave” is consistent with this main theme. An important subsidiary theme in 4:8–10, however, is the triumph of Christ over the evil spiritual powers ranged against God and his people (cf. Arnold 1989: 56–57; Gombis 2005: 375–76). Paul not only describes this triumph explicitly in the quotation’s statement that “he captured captivity,” but he also hints at Christ’s triumph over these powers when, in his interpretation of the quotation, he says that Christ ascended “far above all [ὑπεράνω πάντων, hyperanō pantōn] the heavens” (v. 10). This statement recalls Paul’s earlier claim in 1:20–21 that when God raised Christ from the dead, he seated him “at his right hand in the heavenly places, high above all [ὑπεράνω πάσης, hyperanō pasēs] rule and authority and power and lordship and every name that is named.” Paul’s interest in Ps. 68:18, therefore, lay not only in the “gifts” that the psalm mentions but also in its expression of God’s triumph over his enemies (cf. Col. 2:15).

The notion that God has triumphed over the enemies of his people is also a prominent theme in Ps. 68. The psalm begins with a request that God arise and scatter his enemies (vv. 1–2), continues with a historical review of God’s military triumphs over Israel’s enemies from the exodus to the battle of Deborah and Barak against the forces of Sisera (vv. 7–10; cf. Judg. 5:4–5, 21), and as it reaches its climax (Terrien 2003: 486–87, 490, 494; pace Moritz 1996a: 65–66), pictures God as sweeping all his enemies before him in a dramatic military drive from Mount Sinai to Mount Zion (vv. 17–18). It concludes with references to God’s continued triumph over his enemies and the enemies of his people in the future (vv. 21–23, 28–30). Paul’s quotation comes from the psalm’s triumphant climax in verses 17–18. Although Paul has changed the wording of verse 18, therefore, he has done so in a way that is consistent with the psalm’s theme of God’s triumph over the enemies of his people (cf. Calvin 1965: 174–75; Gombis 2005: 374–76).

[4:9] Paul’s interest in Christ’s triumph becomes explicit in his commentary on the psalm’s reference to an ascent to the height. What could the statement “he ascended” mean, he asks rhetorically, except that “he also descended”? Paul’s use of a rhetorical question here shows that he thinks his conclusion is obvious, but what was obvious to Paul and his readers is no longer so clear.

Does Christ’s ascent make it obvious that he later descended, perhaps in the Spirit given at Pentecost? If so, then 4:11 would fit neatly with developments in the earliest church as they emerge from the Acts narrative. Just as the giving of the Spirit followed Christ’s exaltation to heaven (Acts 2:33), so here Christ ascends to heaven and then gives the gifts of apostles, prophets, evangelists, and teachers to the church (W. H. Harris 1996: 159–60; cf. Abbott 1897: 115–16; Lincoln 1990: 246–47).

Two problems, however, make this reading unlikely. First, in Acts 2 Christ sends the Spirit from heaven to all believers, but in Eph. 4:11 Christ sends certain gifted individuals to the church. Second, Paul makes a special point of saying in 4:10 that it was exactly the same person (αὐτός, autos), Christ, who both ascended and descended, and yet in Ephesians the work of Christ and the work of the Spirit are kept separate. The Spirit makes available to those who believe the gospel what Christ has accomplished (1:13; 2:22).[9]

Does Christ’s ascent, then, make it obvious that he first descended? If this is the correct assumption, then Paul is drawing a conclusion from the widely accepted idea in early Christianity that Christ was with God prior to his manifestation among human beings. If that is true, and yet at some point he “ascended to the height” (Ps. 68:18), then obviously he first had to descend. As the early witnesses that added the term πρῶτον (prōton, first) after κατέβη (katebē, he descended) reveal, this was one of the earliest interpretations of the text (see the additional note). It has in its favor its conformity both to Paul’s conviction, implied earlier in the letter, that Christ was with God before the world’s foundation (1:4; cf. 1 Cor. 8:6) and its correspondence to claims elsewhere in the Pauline corpus that Christ went from a glorious, eternal existence with God to a humble existence among human beings (Phil. 2:6–8; 2 Cor. 8:9). Moreover, when the ascent and descent of Christ are discussed together in John’s Gospel, the ascent is Christ’s return to the place from which he had first descended (John 3:13; 6:33, 41, 50–51, 58, 62). This was apparently the most common way in which early Christians spoke of the “ascent” and “descent” of Christ.

If Paul had simply said that an ascent to the height also involves a descent or had spoken of a descent “to the earth,” this would be the best understanding of the passage. Instead, however, he says that Christ went down εἰς τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς (eis ta katōtera tēs gēs, to the lower regions of the earth). Does this mean that he descended “to the earth’s lower regions” (taking τῆς γῆς as a “partitive” or “possessive” genitive), or does it mean that he descended “to the lower regions, that is, the earth” (taking τῆς γῆς as an “appositional” or “epexegetical” genitive)? Until the late nineteenth century, interpreters of Ephesians understood the phrase as a reference to “the earth’s lower regions.”[10] Christ’s descent would then be to hades, the realm of the dead, thought of as below the earth’s surface.

Why would Christ make such a journey? Perhaps to allow OT saints to become Christians (Tertullian, An. 55.2 [W. H. Harris 1996: 4]; Jerome [Heine 2002: 173]), to give the dead a chance to hear the gospel and be set free (Ambrosiaster, ACCSNT 8:164), or to rescue from the devil’s captivity in limbo the saints who had died before Christ (Aquinas [W. H. Harris 1996: 6]). Or perhaps Paul simply means that Christ went to the place of the dead as a human being who experienced death (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.46]; Westcott 1906: 61; Büchsel, TDNT 3:640–42; Masson 1953: 190; Hoehner 2002: 536; Gombis 2005: 376–78).

Calvin’s patience with all this was clearly wearing thin one Sunday morning in 1558. “Many have made glosses much too strong on this passage,” he told his congregation, “saying that Jesus Christ went down not only into the grave, but also even into limbo, a place forged out of their own brain” (Calvin 1973: 350). Calvin, by contrast, proposed an elegantly simple explanation: Paul spoke of Christ’s incarnation.[11] Although Calvin was not explicit about how he took the grammar of the phrase, he apparently understood τῆς γῆς in an appositional sense and took the larger phrase as a reference to the earth. He was one of the first in a long line of interpreters to do this.[12] By 1883 Eadie (293) could say that this interpretation was the position of “the majority of expositors,” and a century later Schnackenburg (1991: 179n18) claimed that the old descensus ad infernos understanding had “now been abandoned.”

The newer approach apparently solved several problems. First, early Christian literature pictures Christ ascending to heaven from the earth rather than from under the earth (Eadie 1883: 292; Haupt 1902a: 139; Best 1998: 384; cf. Barth 1974: 434). Second, Ephesians has a two-tiered (heaven and earth) rather than a three-tiered (heaven, earth, under the earth) view of the universe (Lincoln 1990: 245; W. H. Harris 1996: 179n26; Best 1998: 384; cf. Haupt 1902a: 139). Third, the enemy powers that Christ has defeated are located not under the earth but in the heavens (Barth 1974: 433), and in Ephesians, Christ defeated these powers at his ascension, not during a descent into hell between his death and resurrection (Barth 1974: 433; Best 1998: 384).

Despite the pleasing simplicity of this reading and the number of problems it seems to solve, however, it probably misconstrues the grammar. The expression τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς is an odd way of referring to the surface of the earth. If Paul had intended to refer to Christ’s (or the Spirit’s) descent merely to the earth, he would have simply written εἰς τὰ κατώτερα (eis ta katōtera, to the lower parts), which would have been ambiguous enough, or εἰς τὴν γῆν (eis tēn gēn, to the earth). The most natural way to take the Greek as it stands is as a reference to subterranean regions (Muddiman 2001: 192–93).

Greco-Roman culture, moreover, was awash with stories of descent to the underworld: Dionysus, Aeneas, Orpheus, and Pythagoras, among others, visited the underworld and lived to tell the tale (Bauckham 1992: 149–54).[13] Relatively ordinary visionaries could sometimes do the same, at least by means of trances and dreams (Bauckham 1992: 151).[14] The myth of Hades carrying Persephone down to the underworld was widely depicted on the coinage of Asia Minor in the first century (Kreitzer 1998b: 388), and locals in Hierapolis pointed a steady stream of tourists to a nearby gas-emitting cave where, they said, the famous abduction had taken place (Casson 1994: 232; Kreitzer 1998b: 388–90). Other “springs, rivers, lakes, caves, chasms, and volcanoes” could also provide access to the chambers of the underworld (Bauckham 1992: 150; cf. Arnold 1989: 57; Kreitzer 1998b: 385–87).[15]

Thus everyone knew that one went “down” to get to the underworld, and various words beginning with the preposition κατά (kata, down) were frequently associated with the realm of the dead. One was brought “down” (κατάγω, katagō; e.g., Gen. 37:35; 42:38; 44:29, 31; 1 Sam. 2:6; 1 Kings 2:6, 9; 1 Clem. 4.12; Lucian, Men. 1, 6) or simply “went down” (καταβαίνω, katabainō; Gen. 37:35 LXX; Num. 16:30, 33 LXX; Aristides of Athens, Apol. 11.3; Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 4.25.4; Artemidorus Daldianus, Oneir. 2.55; cf. BDAG 514) to hades (cf. Rom. 10:6–7), and the path to hades went “downward” (κάτω, katō), below the earth’s surface (e.g., Aristophanes, Ran. 70; Plato, Resp. 10.614c; Deut. 32:22 LXX). Not surprisingly, then, the place of the dead could be referred to simply as τὰ κάτω (ta katō, the [parts] below; Lucian, Men. 2).[16]

It seems extremely unlikely that Paul would use the phrase κατέβη εἰς τὰ κατώτερα τῆς γῆς in such a cultural environment and expect his readers to understand by it anything other than a descent to the realm of the dead (cf. Arnold 1989: 57; Schwindt 2002: 395–96). According to Paul, then, the ascent of Christ inevitably implies his descent to the earth’s lower reaches, the place of the dead.

This brings us back, however, to the original confusion that this interpretation introduces into Paul’s argument. Why is it obvious to Paul that Christ’s ascent implies his descent to the realm of the dead, and what was the purpose for such a descent?

The answers to these questions probably lie in seeing Christ’s descent to the realm of the dead not as something that happened between his death and resurrection, but as part of a single, triumphant event that included his ascent. After his resurrection, Christ both descended into the regions of the dead and ascended to a position above all the heavens. As with Ps. 139:8, the reference to a descent below the earth and an ascent above the heavens is a way of emphasizing the reach of God to every corner of the universe (cf. Jer. 23:24; Jon. 2:2–9; Rom. 10:6–7).[17] In this case, the reach is that of Christ, and its purpose is the defeat and captivity of all the malevolent powers of the universe (v. 8).

It is true that elsewhere in Ephesians the evil spiritual powers are located above the earth, but for Paul they are both in the air (2:2)—the region between earth and heaven—and in the heavenly places (6:12). Clearly he was not concerned about their precise cosmic location (cf. Hanson 1980: 138–39; Schwindt 2002: 396). When he speaks of Christ’s descent to the underworld, he is similarly not concerned with geography but with the common association in antiquity between the realm of the dead and the fear that many people felt of the evils harbored there. Hades was a place of torment (Luke 16:23) and decay (Acts 2:27, 31). To some, its entrance was guarded by the menacing goddess Hecate, “supreme,” says Virgil, “both in Heaven and in Hell” (caeloque Ereboque potentem; Aen. 6.247, trans. Fairclough and Goold 1999–2000).[18] Hades himself was “dark and sinister, a god to be feared and kept at a distance” (Henrichs 2003a: 661; cf. Rev. 6:8; 20:14). Evil spirits, the offspring of the illicit union between rebellious angels and human women (cf. Gen. 6:1–4), existed “inside the earth” (1 En. 15.8–10 [OTP 1:21–22]), and rebellious angels were imprisoned in subterranean cavities, awaiting their final doom on judgment day (1 En. 10.12 [OTP 1:18]; cf. Jude 6, 13; 2 Pet. 2:4, 17).

All such powers, says Paul, in whatever corner of the cosmos they may cringe, are now conquered and have taken their place beneath Christ’s feet (1:22). The thought is similar to Phil. 2:10, where at the name of Jesus every knee bows, whether heavenly (ἐπουρανίων, epouraniōn), earthly (ἐπιγείων, epigeiōn), or subterranean (καταχθονίων, katachthoniōn). It is also similar to 1 Pet. 3:19–22, where on the most probable interpretation, Christ preaches condemnation to imprisoned evil spirits and subjects “angels and authorities and powers” to himself before taking his seat at God’s right hand (cf. Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 11; NPNF 13:103–4).

[4:10] Paul completes this thought with two assertions about Christ’s ascent and descent. First, he says that the one who descended and the one who ascended are identical with each other.[19] He does this not to make a christological point about the identity of the incarnate with the heavenly Christ (pace, e.g., Jerome [Heine 2002: 174]; Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.46]; Eadie 1883: 295), nor to make a pastoral point about the identity of the exalted Christ with the Spirit who is present in the church (pace W. H. Harris 1996: 182). Instead, the assertion that the Christ who ascended is identical with the Christ who descended prepares the way for the statement in 4:11 that the very one who both descended and ascended is the one who gave gifts to the church. This is why the emphatic αὐτός in 4:10 is repeated in 4:11. The Christ who is powerful enough to conquer the enemies of God’s people in every corner of the universe is also the Christ who equips God’s people to fulfill their destiny of full union with him. If he was strong enough for one task, he is strong enough for the other.

Second, Paul brings verses 7–10 to a conclusion with a statement of the purpose for Christ’s descent and ascent. He descended to the earth’s lower regions and ascended far above the heavens so that, like God himself in verse 6, he might fill all things (Aletti 2001: 217). The picture is similar to that of 1:20–23, where Christ is seated at God’s right hand “in the heavenly places, high above” the malevolent powers who lie subjected beneath his feet. This victory was not merely for himself but also for the church, which as his body joins him in filling every corner of the universe (1:23). Having recalled the theme of Christ’s universal victory over evil, Paul will now, in 4:11–16, show how the gifts that the victorious Christ gives to the church aid it in growing into unity with himself and thus, like him, filling all things (v. 15; cf. Bruce 1984: 344–45).

[4:11] Christ, who has extended his victory over all opposing forces and his sovereignty over all creation, is the very one who (αὐτός, autos, he himself) now equips the church to join him in his sovereign reign over all creation (cf. 2:6; 4:15). He does this through giving gifts to discrete groups of people (v. 11) so they, in turn, can equip others to serve and edify the church (v. 12). Although the syntax of the list of gifted groups is complex and disputed, the most plausible understanding of the text places the emphasis less on the positions that certain people hold in the church and more on the activities that Christ has equipped certain people to perform (see the additional note). Paul lists five groups of these people.

First, he has given τοὺς μέν (tous men, some) to be ἀποστόλους (apostolous, apostles). The apostles and prophets together form the foundation of the new multiethnic people of God (2:20), a position that belongs to them because of their critical role in taking the gospel to the Gentiles (3:5). Of the two groups, however, the apostles are always mentioned first, and in 3:5 they are described as both “holy” and as Christ’s apostles. They hold this place of greatest foundational importance because of their connection with the historical Jesus (see the comments on 3:5). Paul numbers himself among the apostles, although he considers himself to be the last and least of them (1 Cor. 15:8–9; see the comments on 1:1; 2:20; and 3:5).

Second, Christ has given τοὺς δέ (tous de, others) to be προφήτας (prophētas, prophets). As we saw above in the comments on 2:20, these prophets are not OT prophets but people living in Paul’s own time who were prompted by the Spirit to speak a particularly relevant message to an individual (1 Cor. 14:24–25) or to the church (Acts 11:27–30; 15:32; 21:10–11). The messages that prophets communicate seem to come at particularly critical moments in the lives of people or in the history of the church. The Spirit reveals “mysteries” to prophets that they then communicate to the church for its edification and encouragement (1 Cor. 13:2; 14:3–4, 31) and that they communicate to unbelievers for their conversion (14:24–25). Among these mysteries is God’s plan to include the Gentiles as equal partners with the Jews as his people (Eph. 3:5–6; cf. Acts 13:1–3; 15:22, 32; cf. 19:6), and this particular role may have led Paul to give them a place of importance in his list second only to that of apostles. Paul’s Gentile readers have heard and believed the gospel and so have become part of God’s people because of the foundational witness of apostles and prophets.

Third, Christ has given “others” (τοὺς δέ) to be εὐαγγελιστάς (euangelistas, evangelists). The general meaning of the term is fairly obvious: it refers to one who brings good news, and since it is apparently of Christian coinage (TLNT 2:91), the good news proclaimed is the Christian gospel of peace with God through Christ’s crucifixion (2:17; cf. 1:13; 3:6, 8; 6:15, 19). The term is used in the NT, however, in only two other places, neither of them very illuminating about its precise meaning (Acts 21:8; 2 Tim. 4:5). If we use the closely related terms εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion, good news) and εὐαγγελίζω (euangelizō, bring good news) to help define εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistēs, evangelist), we can be more specific. These other terms typically refer to glad tidings that reach people after messengers have traveled to bring the tidings to them. People make the “rounds” with the “good news” that an enemy’s king has been killed in battle (κύκλῳ εὐαγγελίζοντες, kyklō euangelizontes; 1 Sam. 31:9 [par. 1 Chron. 10:9] LXX; cf. 2 Sam. 18:19–31 LXX; Josephus, Ant. 18.228–29), or return home with the good news of diplomatic success (Josephus, Ant. 11.65; 15.209). The good news of an emperor’s accession spreads through the world (Josephus, J.W. 4.618, 656). Messengers run from one place to another to deliver good news (2 Sam. 18:19; Nah. 2:1 LXX, MT [1:15 Eng.]; Isa. 52:7), and ambassadors travel from place to place with it (Josephus, J.W. 2.418–20). Angels bring good news from heaven to earth (Luke 1:19). Jesus travels around Judea (Luke 4:43) and Galilee (Matt. 4:23; 9:35; Luke 8:1) proclaiming it. His followers take it everywhere (Mark 13:10; 14:9; Matt. 24:14; 26:13; cf. Luke 9:6). In Ephesians, we read that Jesus “came” and proclaimed the good news of peace (2:17), and the gospel of peace is connected with the feet of believers (6:15). One can certainly tell good news without traveling (Pss. 39:10 LXX [40:10 MT; 40:9 Eng.]; 67:12 [68:12 MT; 68:11 Eng.]; 95:2 [96:2 MT, Eng.]), but the most characteristic uses of the noun εὐαγγέλιον and the verb εὐαγγελίζω involve the element of traveling.

“Evangelists,” then, are probably those whom God has especially equipped to travel from place to place with the good news of peace through Christ. Although both Philip and Timothy are settled in one place when they are called “evangelists” (Acts 21:8; 2 Tim. 4:5; Best 1997a: 165), Philip has traveled around preaching the gospel (Acts 8:4–5, 35, 40), and Paul is ready for Timothy to pull up stakes and travel again (2 Tim. 4:9, 21). Paul, then, probably thinks of “evangelists” as similar to apostles but without their authority because of their lack of direct connection to the historical Jesus (Friedrich, TDNT 2:737). The evangelists proclaim the message to which the apostles have been eye- and earwitnesses (cf. Eusebius Hist. eccl. 5.10.2; Schnackenburg 1991: 181).

The fourth and fifth gifts that Christ gives his church body, unlike the first three, are linked together with καί and share a single τοὺς δέ construction: τοὺς δὲ ποιμένας καὶ διδασκάλους (tous de poimenas kai didaskalous, others to be pastors and teachers). This variation from the pattern has occasioned two interpretive debates.

First, some earlier commentators thought these two groups were linked together because they were attached to a local congregation, whereas the first three groups (apostles, prophets, and evangelists) traveled from place to place (e.g., Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 11; NPNF 13:104; Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.46]; Ellicott 1859: 87; Abbott 1897: 118; Robinson 1904: 181). Not all apostles and prophets, however, conducted itinerant ministries. James the Lord’s brother was an apostle but stayed in Jerusalem (1 Cor. 15:7; Gal. 1:18–19; Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18), and there is no evidence that the Corinthian prophets (1 Cor. 11:2–16; 14:1–40) traveled anywhere.

Second, some interpreters think that the single τοὺς δέ construction means that the pastors and teachers were the same people with two sets of skills (e.g., Alford 1857: 113; Eadie 1883: 304; Barth 1974: 438). The common τοὺς δέ, however, does not require this interpretation. Paul used one article to modify “apostles” and “prophets” in 2:20, for example, but apparently considered them to be separate groups (cf. Best 1997a: 168; Hoehner 2002: 543–44). Paul may have intended to imply that “pastors” and “teachers” were overlapping although not entirely identical groups. It is also possible that the τοὺς δέ was simply “dropped as unnecessarily tedious repetition” (Muddiman 2001: 199). Whatever the reason for the missing τοὺς δέ, the evidence is not clear enough to allow us to consider “pastors” and “teachers” as a single group.

The term ποιμήν (poimēn) simply means “shepherd” and was often used metaphorically for a political or religious leader in the ancient Near East (Jeremias, TDNT 6:486–87; Block 1998: 279–81). In the OT, too, God is often portrayed as a shepherd who tends his sheep, the people of Israel (e.g., Gen. 48:15; Pss. 23:1–4; 80:1; Isa. 40:11; 49:9–10; Jer. 50:19; Zech. 10:8–9; Jeremias, TDNT 6:487; Block 1998: 284–85). When Moses prays for a man to lead Israel so that they “may not be like sheep without a shepherd” (NRSV), the Lord answers the prayer with Joshua (Num. 27:16–18; Block 1998: 281). King David is said to “shepherd” Israel (2 Sam. 5:2 [1 Chron. 11:2]; Ps. 78:70–72; Jeremias, TDNT 6:488n30), and God will come through a future “David” and shepherd his people (Ezek. 34:11, 23–24; cf. Jer. 23:1–6; cf. Pss. Sol. 17.40; Jeremias, TDNT 6:489). The metaphor also appears in Greek literature for a leader or king (e.g., Homer, Il. 2.85, 243; LSJ 1430). The Gospels sometimes picture Jesus as a shepherd who has compassion on the wandering flock of God’s people (Matt. 10:6; 15:24; Luke 15:4–7; John 10:3, 11–14, 27; cf. Ezek. 34:11–16), and the metaphor reappears in 1 Pet. 2:25 (cf. Heb. 13:20; Jeremias, TDNT 6:490, 492, 494).

First Peter 5:1–4 explicitly connects Jesus’s role as a shepherd with the work of “elders” (πρεσβύτεροι, presbyteroi), who should “shepherd the flock of God” (5:2 ESV) for the right motives, without being authoritarian, and by setting an example “for the flock” with their own behavior (5:3). If they shepherd their flocks this way, then the chief shepherd (ἀρχιποίμην, archipoimēn), Jesus, will reward them when he appears (5:4).

All this means that in Eph. 4:11 the ποιμένες (poimenes, shepherds/pastors) were probably leaders within Christian communities who held positions of authority and were charged with the community’s well-being.[20] Since the wicked shepherds of the OT led God’s people astray (Jer. 23:1–2; Ezek. 34:1–6), perhaps by the second half of the first century, Christian shepherds were especially concerned with protecting the flock from the “savage wolves” who invaded Christian communities such as Ephesus with false teaching (Acts 20:28–30; Matt. 7:15; cf. Eph. 4:14; Ezek. 22:27).

If the τοὺς δέ in front of ποιμένας and the καί after it were intended to join ποιμένας to διδασκάλους (didaskalous, teachers), a concern to keep false teaching at bay may be the reason Paul coupled these two groups. Later, he will say that as a result of the maturity toward which these five groups of leaders are leading the church, believers will “no longer be infants, wave-tossed and blown around by every wind of teaching, by human trickery, by cunning, in the service of the system of error” (4:14). Since the problem identified here is false teaching, the “teachers” of whom Paul speaks in 4:11 will play a particularly critical role in attaining this goal.

The first four groups in Paul’s list will all have been teachers; indeed, there was a sense in which all Christians were to teach each other (Col. 3:16; Heb. 5:12; Best 1997a: 166–67). Nevertheless, as Paul’s earliest extant correspondence shows, there was a group of people in the church who specialized in teaching (1 Thess. 5:12; cf. Gal. 6:6; 1 Cor. 12:28; Rom. 12:7; Acts 13:1; James 3:1; Best 1997a: 166; BDAG 241).[21] Insofar as we can distinguish “teachers” from “shepherds,” we should probably think of people who are not necessarily skilled in administration (Ellicott 1859: 87), but whom Christ has equipped to instruct others in what 1 Tim. 6:1 calls “the teaching” (ἡ διδασκαλία, hē didaskalia), “the Christian message or doctrine by which the church is known” (Towner 2006: 382). In Ephesians, to sit under this teaching is simply to “learn Christ” (4:20; Best 1997a: 166–67), a phrase that probably refers to learning the basics of the gospel about Christ as well as its ethical implications (5:2).

[4:12] Paul next dictated three prepositional phrases whose relationship to the five groups in 4:11 is unclear and whose interpretation has become the subject of sometimes heated debate. There are two main views of how these prepositional phrases function, although each main view has given birth to several variations.[22] The dispute focuses on how the middle phrase, εἰς ἔργον διακονίας (eis ergon diakonias, for the work of ministry), should be understood.

The first view takes this phrase as coordinate with the preceding phrase πρὸς τὸν καταρτισμὸν τῶν ἁγίων (pros ton katartismon tōn hagiōn), which is translated as “for the equipping of the saints.” On this view, the apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers not only bring the saints to full maturity, but they also do the work of ministry.

The second view claims that the phrase εἰς ἔργον διακονίας fills out the meaning of the term καταρτισμόν (katartismon), now translated as “preparation” or “equipping.” The five groups of verse 11, then, prepare or equip the saints “for the work of ministry.”

The temperature of the debate begins to rise when interpreters suspect that the exegesis of the text has been driven more by concerns about the structure of the modern church than by dispassionate scholarship. According to this text, who does the work of ministry in today’s church: the officers of the church or the people whom the officers equip?

The first view is ancient, going back at least as far as Chrysostom (PG 62:85; cf., e.g., John of Damascus, PG 95:841, 843; Calvin 1965: 180–81) and is exegetically well supported.
