In its basic form, it takes all three prepositional phrases as coordinate with each other and sees each as a modifier of the verb ἔδωκεν (edōken, he gave) in verse 11. The three phrases describe three purposes for which Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers to the church. He gave them



for (πρός, pros) the “equipping” of the saints

for (εἰς, eis) [the] work of ministry

for (εἰς) [the] edification of the body of Christ.



Supporters of this view argue that it fits the stylistic character of Ephesians since in this letter strings of coordinate prepositional phrases often modify a verb without coordinating conjunctions (Lincoln 1990: 253; Muddiman 2001: 200; Page 2005: 30–32). In 1:3, for example, God blesses believers “with [ἐν, en] every spiritual blessing in [ἐν] the heavenly places in [ἐν] Christ,” and in 1:5–6 God has predetermined believers “for [εἰς, eis] adoptive sonship by means of [διά, dia] Jesus Christ, for [εἰς, eis] him[self], according to [κατά, kata] the pleasure of his will, for [εἰς] the praise of his glorious grace” (cf. 1:20–21; 2:7; 4:13–14; 6:12).

In addition, those who hold this view think that it makes the best sense of the term διακονία (diakonia, ministry) in the phrase “for the work of ministry” (e.g., Schnackenburg 1991: 183; Gordon 1994: 75–77; O’Neill 2001: 336–40; Page 2005: 35–40). This term often appears in Paul’s Letters and elsewhere in the NT as a reference to “the ministry of the word” and frequently seems to carry an official nuance (Acts 6:4; cf. 2 Cor. 3:6–8; 4:1; 5:18; 6:3; Rom. 11:13; Acts 20:24; 21:19; 1 Tim. 1:12; 2 Tim. 4:5). The “work of ministry,” therefore, probably belongs to the five groups listed in verse 11, all of whom fill roles that involve communicating the gospel and its implications to others.

This view, however, faces serious syntactical and contextual difficulties. Syntactically, it is true that Ephesians frequently modifies verbs with strings of prepositional phrases, but these strings are sometimes as ambiguous as this one. For example, in the phrase “having predestined us for adoptive sonship through Christ Jesus” in 1:5, does the phrase through Christ Jesus go with “predestined” or with “adoptive sonship”? A similar ambiguity arises in 2:7; 4:14; and 6:12. The only strings of prepositional phrases where this ambiguity does not arise are those whose prepositional objects contain no verbal idea (1:3, 20–21; 4:13). Here in 4:12, however, the noun καταρτισμός is a verbal noun and could easily itself be modified by a prepositional phrase to indicate the purpose of its implied verbal action.

The prepositional phrases, moreover, are not syntactically parallel. This lack of parallelism is not merely a matter of the shift from πρός to εἰς, which could be a stylistic variation (so Page 2005: 30). In addition, the object of πρός has an article whereas the objects of εἰς have no article.[23]

Contextually, 4:7–16 is concerned with the role of all believers in the unity of the church. In verse 7 at the beginning of the passage, “each one” (ἑνὶ . . . ἑκάστῳ, heni . . . hekastō) receives grace “according to the measure [μέτρον, metron]” that Christ decides. This matches the focus of verse 16 at the end of the passage when it says that “each single [ἑνὸς ἑκάστου, henos hekastou] part” assists the body in its growth “in the measure” (μέτρῳ, metrō) for which it has been empowered (cf. De Wette 1843: 135; Westcott 1906: 62–63; O’Brien 1999: 303; Hoehner 2002: 549).[24]

It is true that the five groups of verse 11 are equipped with mainly verbal gifts and are therefore engaged in what Paul, in other contexts, refers to as the special “ministry” of communicating the gospel. In verse 15, however, we discover that all believers should speak the truth in love, and this refers primarily to speaking to others “the word of truth, the gospel of . . . salvation” (1:13), and in 4:29 everyone is to be ready to use their words for the edification (οἰκοδομή, oikodomē) of others where the need exists. In 1 Cor. 12:4–7, moreover, the term “ministries” (διακονίαι, diakoniai) stands parallel to “gifts” and “activities,” and all three are manifestations of the Spirit given “to each person . . . for the common good.”

Is this view of “the work of ministry” in 4:12 a relatively recent innovation that is suspiciously supportive of the egalitarian and democratic spirit popular in some circles at the end of the twentieth century (Lincoln 1990: 253; Gordon 1994: 77; Muddiman 2001: 200)?[25] It would be difficult to make this charge stick. Scholars as early and diverse as De Wette (1843: 135), Robinson (1904: 182), and Westcott (1906: 62–63) have argued for forms of this view. Westcott’s (1906: 63) remarks are particularly instructive: “However foreign the idea of the spiritual ministry of all ‘the saints’ is to our mode of thinking,” he says, “it was the life of the apostolic church.” The idea was perhaps especially foreign to Westcott since he was bishop of Durham when he penned these words.[26]

The second view, then, is probably correct. The three prepositional phrases build on each other, and the apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers of 4:11 equip all believers to do the work of ministry for the edification of Christ’s body.

If this is right, then the term καταρτισμός (katartismos) has less the nuance of “completing” or “perfecting” the saints than of “equipping” them for a particular purpose. The noun is rare, appearing only here in the NT and seldom outside of medical texts prior to the first century. Its medical use refers to the straightening or setting of a joint or broken bone.[27] It also appears in nonliterary texts from roughly the time of Ephesians, where it refers to “outfitting” a guest room with furniture, the “equipment” that goes along with a couple of beds, and the “preparation” of woof and warp necessary for weaving a garment (MM 332; NewDocs 3:70, no. 42). Paul uses the term here with this last meaning: the saints are prepared εἰς ἔργον διακονίας (eis ergon diakonias, for the work of ministry).[28] Christ has given the five groups of verse 11 to the church for the “equipping” or “preparation” of the saints, and the purpose of this preparation was that the saints might do the work of ministry.[29]

The ultimate goal of the preparation of the saints and the work of their ministry is the οἰκοδομὴ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (oikodomē tou sōmatos tou Christou, the building up of the body of Christ). Οἰκοδομή is reminiscent of 2:20–22, where the “building” (οἰκοδομή) under construction is the “dwelling place” (κατοικητήριον, katoikētērion) of God. Its foundation is the apostles and prophets, Christ is its guiding and crowning stone, and its building blocks are believers from both Jews and Gentiles. Here the same idea is under consideration, but now evangelists, pastors, and teachers are involved in addition to apostles and prophets, and their job is to equip all believers (“the saints”) to participate in the construction.[30] Already in 2:21 the architectural metaphor had started to break out of its boundaries when Paul says that the “building . . . grows” (οἰκοδομὴ . . . αὔξει, oikodomē . . . auxei). Here too the metaphor suddenly becomes organic since believers are constructing not a building but “the body of Christ,” a metaphor Paul has already explained as referring to “the church” (1:22–23; cf. 5:23).

To summarize, the ascended and triumphant Christ has given an appropriate measure of grace to each believer. Among those whom he has gifted, Paul lists five groups especially equipped to prepare other believers for the work of ministry: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers. Those gifted in the ministry of the word and those whom they equip for ministry work together to build up the body of Christ.

[4:13] Paul next describes the final goal of this construction work as union with Christ in all his fullness. The first clause of the verse, μέχρι καταντήσωμεν οἱ πάντες (mechri katantēsōmen hoi pantes, until we all arrive), should be attached not to the verb ἔδωκεν (edōken, he gave) in 4:11 (pace Hoehner 2002: 552) but to the verbal idea contained in the closer noun οἰκοδομήν (oikodomēn, building up). Paul is not saying that Christ continues to give apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers to the church “until we all arrive,” but that the work of building up the church continues “until we all arrive.” The article οἱ (hoi) with πάντες (pantes, all) emphasizes that the whole is made up of individuals. It “gathers all the particulars under one view” (Robinson 1904: 182; cf. 1 Cor. 10:17; Rom. 11:32). The picture is of all believers employing the gifts Christ has given to them in order to reach a goal that will likewise involve them all.

What is this goal? Paul describes it in three parallel prepositional phrases, each beginning with εἰς (eis, at).[31] Unlike the three prepositional phrases in 4:12, these phrases do not build on each other but view the same result from different angles.[32]

First, Paul describes the goal of building up the body of Christ as arriving “at the unity [ἑνότητα, henotēta] of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God.” Those who equip the saints for the work of ministry in 4:11 are all teachers, and in 4:14–15 Paul will say that a sign of the maturity toward which the church is moving is its purity from false teaching. “The unity of the faith,” then, refers to unity in acknowledging a particular body of doctrine, the “one faith” of 4:5.

“Knowledge [ἐπίγνωσις, epignōsis] of the Son of God” is more difficult to define. The term ἐπίγνωσις appears elsewhere in the letter only in 1:17, where it refers to knowing God in a way that only he can make possible through the work of his Spirit. In this letter, “knowing” often means understanding the “mystery”—God’s plan to unite the universe around Christ (1:9–10; 3:3, 5–6, 9–10; 6:19). Perhaps here, then, the compound term ἐπίγνωσις refers to a personal, experiential knowledge of God’s Son, around whom God’s plan for the universe revolves (cf. Phil. 3:8–11). If this is right, then in this first εἰς phrase Paul describes the goal of “the building up of the body of Christ” as the unity of all its parts in a common set of doctrines and in a common experience of knowing the Christ on whom those doctrines are focused (cf. Aletti 2001: 222).

Second, Paul describes this goal as ἄνδρα τέλειον (andra teleion, a mature man). Earlier Paul said that Christ, in his death, has abolished the Mosaic law so that he might “create” Gentiles and Jews “into one new human being [ἄνθρωπον, anthrōpon] in him” (2:15). He then portrays these two groups of believers as coming together to form a “building” (οἰκοδομή) that, “being joined together, grows [αὔξει, auxei] into a holy temple in the Lord” (2:21). Here in 4:13 Paul recalls this mixture of architectural and organic imagery: the end result of “building up the body of Christ” (v. 12) is “a mature man.” Like the imagery in 2:15, 21, then, the “mature man” here is a reference not to the individual believer but to the church.

There are important differences, however, between the uses of this imagery in the two passages. One difference is that unlike ἄνθρωπος in 2:15, the expression here is gender and age specific: ἀνήρ (anēr) refers to “an adult human male” (BDAG 79). This may simply be the result of Paul’s desire to contrast human maturity with human immaturity, since in the next verse he will say that once all believers have arrived at the goal of maturity, they will no longer be “infants” (νήπιοι, nēpioi). In addition, however, he may be looking ahead to 5:29–32, where he compares the relationship between Christ and the church with the Genesis narrative’s description of the relationship between husband and wife (Gen. 2:24). It is true that in 5:29–32 the church is the wife of the ἀνήρ rather than the ἀνήρ himself, as here, but it is also important to remember that the main point of 5:29–32 is the unity of man and woman in one flesh, just as here the church and Christ are one body.

Another difference is that in 2:15 the unity of Gentile and Jewish believers in “one new human being” has been accomplished for them by Christ’s death. Here in 4:13 the unity of the church is something that lies in the future and involves the practical effort of exercising the gifts that Christ has given to the church so that believers might “build” it “up” (cf. 4:3).

Paul’s third prepositional phrase affirms that believers must build up the body until it reaches μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (metron hēlikias tou plērōmatos tou Christou, the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ). This phrase could refer to reaching the mature age of Christ, an idea that the references to maturity in the previous phrase and to children in the next verse seem at first to support (Calvin 1965: 182; Abbott 1897: 120). But the phrase can also refer to the height of a person such as the mature man of the previous phrase, and this is probably Paul’s emphasis (Alford 1857: 114; Ellicott 1859: 90).[33] Both the reference to “fullness” in this verse and the image of growth in verse 15 point in this direction, and the idea of measurement also coheres better than its alternative with the architectural metaphor that still hovers in the background from verse 12. Paul, then, intends for his readers to think of the church, which is the body of Christ, as eventually attaining Christ’s full height.

The meaning of this image becomes clear if we remember what Paul has said in 1:20–23; 2:4–6 and in the present context, 4:8–10. Christ has conquered all the evil spiritual forces of the universe by filling every corner of the universe, whether high or low (1:20–22; 4:8–10). There is a sense in which believers have already joined him in this victory since they are his body (1:23) and are united with him in his heavenly place of victory at God’s right hand (2:6). We now learn, however, that there is also a sense in which the church’s union with Christ is not yet complete. Christ has already filled the universe (4:10), but the church is still moving toward full union with Christ in this specific sense. The Ruler of the realm of the air is still at work among the sons of disobedience (2:2); the waves and winds of false teaching still trouble the church (4:14); basic moral instruction is still necessary (4:17–6:9); and believers still need to be armed against the devil’s strategies (6:10–20). These challenges mean that believers must exercise the gifts that Christ has given them and work to build up the church until it attains the full union with the victorious Christ that God intends for it.

[4:14] Paul’s next clause provides a negative contrast to the positive picture of the church’s destiny in verse 13.[34] The church’s goal, negatively viewed, is to move believers out of childhood, with its susceptibility to various false teachings (v. 14). The term νήπιοι (nēpioi, infants) stands in sharp contrast to the ἀνήρ τέλειος (anēr teleios, mature man) of verse 13. The νήπιοι are many and, by their very nature, immature, but the ἀνήρ is both one and τέλειος. A church moving toward full unity with Christ is leaving behind immaturity, with its intertwined characteristics of ignorance (cf. 1 Cor. 13:11; 14:20; Rom. 2:20; Col. 1:28), gullibility (cf. Heb. 5:12–14), and individualism (cf. 1 Cor. 2:6; 3:1–4; Phil. 3:15).

In this passage Paul is particularly concerned about the vulnerability of the spiritually immature to false teaching. He brings out this emphasis by suddenly switching his metaphor from the stages of human development to that of a storm at sea. Just as in Luke 8:24 Jesus calms a gale whose two components are “the wind [ἀνέμῳ, anemō] and the surge [κλύδωνι, klydōni] of the water,” so here the children of whom Paul speaks are “wave-tossed [κλυδωνιζόμενοι, klydōnizomenoi] and blown around by every wind [ἀνέμῳ, anemō] of teaching.” It was perhaps the changeable, seemingly random, and potentially dangerous aspects of the weather that made it a metaphor of choice for doubt and false teaching in early Christianity (James 1:6; Jude 12; cf. Muddiman 2001: 205). In contrast to the focused and skillfully led church that is moving toward maturity in 4:13, the children of whom Paul speaks here follow a variety of teachings and lack any clear direction (cf. Lincoln 1990: 258).

These doctrinal ill winds toss and blow their victims around ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων (en tē kybeia tōn anthrōpōn, by human trickery). The term κυβεία (kybeia) literally means “dice-playing” (LSJ 1004) but also adopted the connotation simply of cheating and deceit. Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.19.28; 3.21.22) used the verb κυβεύω (kybeuō) to refer to philosophical cheating—claiming to be a philosopher but living in a way that belies the claim (BDAG 573). Paul uses the noun here in a similar way to say that the spiritually immature are gullible, carried away by the teaching of fakes who are playing dishonest games with serious religious matters (cf. Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.21.8–24]). The genitive phrase τῶν ἀνθρώπων is probably intended adjectivally, and it is certainly intended negatively. This deception has nothing to do with God; it is merely “human” (cf. Isa. 29:13 LXX; Gal. 1:11; BDAG 81). Although Paul’s comments are general enough to fit a range of false teachings, he must have had in mind especially the “philosophy” at Colossae, which he also characterizes as merely “human” (Col. 2:8, 22; cf. Lincoln 1990: 258).

The next phrase probably does not build on the one before it but backs up and says the same thing in a single word (cf. Hoehner 2002: 562). The winds that blow the immature here and there do so ἐν πανουργίᾳ (en panourgia, by cunning). Elsewhere Paul uses this term to describe those who knowingly falsify the word of God (2 Cor. 4:2) and to describe Satan’s shrewd deception of Eve (2 Cor. 11:3). It has precisely these connotations here. The immature are susceptible to deception by those who know how to use ruthless but clever tactics.

Paul’s final phrase describes the goal (πρός, pros, for) of the various false teachings as ἡ μεθοδεία τῆς πλάνης (hē methodeia tēs planēs, the system of error). The term μεθοδεία is rare, apparently appearing here and in 6:11 for the first time in extant Greek literature.[35] It is often thought to carry sinister connotations (e.g., Abbott 1897: 122; Hoehner 2002: 563; BDAG 625), but when we next meet it in the second-century mathematical writer Claudius Ptolemaeus, it simply means a particular “method” of mathematical calculation (Syntaxis mathematica I.2:581, line 10).[36] Moreover, although its closely related verb could occasionally be used in a negative way (2 Sam. 19:28 LXX; Polybius, Hist. 38.12.10; Chariton, Chaer. 7.6.10),[37] it most often means simply to “treat or practice by rule or method” (LSJ 1091). Philo frequently uses it this way, and only this way, in his writings (Moses 2.212; Eternity 149; Agriculture 25; Providence 2.60; Worse 109). The term contributes to the phrase, then, not so much a sinister note as the idea of an intentional, organized approach to something.

The sinister element comes from the genitive phrase τῆς πλάνης (tēs planēs) that qualifies τὴν μεθοδείαν (tēn methodeian, the system). Although this term too could have an innocent meaning,[38] Paul uses it elsewhere of a planned deception (1 Thess. 2:3; cf. Matt. 27:64) and of an ethical deviation (Rom. 1:27). It could also refer to doctrinal error (2 Thess. 2:11; 2 Pet. 3:17; 1 John 4:6; Jude 11; cf. James 5:20), and that is the connotation it carries here. The genitive case probably gives the noun an adjectival force, just as τῶν ἀνθρώπων describes κυβείᾳ adjectivally in the preceding phrase. The false teachings that trouble immature believers were concocted in the service of “the system of error.” Despite their variety, the false teachings of which Paul speaks serve one great, erroneous plan (Muddiman 2001: 207), and Paul probably thinks of this plan as guided by “the Ruler of the realm of the air, . . . the spirit now powerfully working in the sons of disobedience” (2:2; cf. 6:11).

In sum, Paul tells his readers that when the church’s gifted teachers use their gifts to equip all believers for the work of ministry, the church progresses toward maturity. It also moves steadily away from immaturity with its fragmentation and susceptibility to deception by cunning theological cheats.

[4:15] Paul now views the same progress toward maturity from a positive perspective. The verb αὐξήσωμεν (auxēsōmen, we might grow) stands in contrast to the phrase μηκέτι ὦμεν (mēketi ōmen, might no longer be) in verse 14 and, like it, is part of the purpose clause that begins with ἵνα (hina, that; v. 14). In contrast (δέ, de, but) to the deceit of the false teachings and the cunning with which they advance “the system of error,” believers grow toward maturity as they speak the truth in love.

Ἀληθεύοντες (alētheuontes) is a participle of means, defining more closely the verb αὐξήσωμεν and describing the way in which the growth takes place. Ἀληθεύοντες does not simply mean “cherishing the truth” (Ellicott 1859: 93; cf. Abbott 1897: 123; Robinson 1904: 185) but refers specifically to speaking the truth. This is clear not only from Gal. 4:16, where ἀληθεύω (alētheuō) refers to telling the truth, but also from the use of the noun ἀλήθεια (alētheia) in Eph. 1:13, where the truth is something that people hear (cf. Gen. 42:16; Isa. 44:26 LXX; NewDocs 4:145, no. 47). In both instances the truth is specifically the truth of the gospel (cf. Gal. 2:5, 14). In contrast to “the error” of verse 14, then, Paul’s readers should grow toward maturity by speaking the gospel truth to others.

The manner in which believers are to speak the truth to others also contrasts with the methods by which the false teachings of verse 13 operate. Whereas their “system of error” proceeds “by trickery” (ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ, en tē kybeia) and “by cunning” (ἐν πανουργίᾳ, en panourgia), believers are to speak the truth “in love” (ἐν ἀγάπῃ, en agapē).[39] Love involves seeking the benefit of the undeserving, even at one’s own expense (2:4–5; 3:19; 5:2, 25; cf. Gal. 2:20b) and is bound up with humility, gentleness, and a willingness to work for unity and peace (Eph. 4:2–3). As those who have heard and believed the gospel themselves (1:13), Paul’s readers are rooted and grounded in this kind of love (3:17; Best 1998: 407), and so they bear witness to the gospel not only by their faithfulness in representing it accurately but also by their motives and manner as they convey its message.

As believers speak the truth in love, they “grow up to him” (αὐξήσωμεν εἰς αὐτόν, auxēsōmen eis auton). The figure is organic, referring to the growth of human beings from childhood (cf. νήπιοι, nēpioi, infants; v. 14) toward maturity. It therefore goes back to the picture of the church arriving eventually “at [εἰς, eis] a mature man” by growing to the size of Christ’s full stature. Its use of the term αὐξάνω/αὔξω (auxanō/auxō, grow) is also reminiscent of the last use of that term in 2:21, where the “building” (οἰκοδομή, oikodomē) of God’s people, comprised of both Jews and Gentiles, “grows [αὔξει, auxei] into [εἰς, eis] a holy temple in the Lord.” This in turn is reminiscent of the use of the term οἰκοδομή in 4:12 to speak of the purpose for which the victorious Christ has given gifts to all his people. He has done so for the “building up” of his body. These connections help us to understand what Paul means when he says that when believers speak the truth in love, they grow “up to” (εἰς) Christ with respect to all things: they are moving closer to the full union with Christ that is the church’s eventual destiny.[40]

Perhaps to prevent the conclusion that the church is moving toward a union with Christ in which the distinction between the church and Christ is dissolved, Paul adds that Christ is “the head” (cf. 1:22; 5:23; cf. Col. 1:18; 2:19). Believers are not, then, growing “into the head,” as some commentators think (e.g., Muddiman 2001: 208).[41] Instead, they are growing “up to Christ” in the sense of verse 13, but Christ, they must not forget, is still the head of his body, the church.

[4:16] Paul now skillfully concludes the section by returning to the theme of Christ’s gifts to every believer so that each one might contribute to building up the church. He does this by placing special emphasis on two themes, both articulated in terms of the metaphors of a growing body and building that he has been using since verse 12.

First, Christ is the source of the church’s “bodily” growth. Just as in verses 7–11 the victorious Christ was the source of the gifts given to each believer for the church’s edification, so here Christ is the one “from whom” (ἐξ οὗ, ex hou) the growth of the body comes. Since Paul has just spoken of Christ as “the head,” he probably thinks of the head of the body as the control center of the body’s growth, a concept that would correspond to at least some ancient physiological thinking about the function of the brain (Lloyd 1973: 77; Dawes 1998: 129–33; pace Bedale 1956: 68). Christ, as the head of the body, “produces” (ποιεῖται, poieitai) the growth of the body. He does this “for its own edification [οἰκοδομήν, oikodomēn].” Here the use of οἰκοδομή recalls both the use of this term in verse 12, where it leads into the figure of the church’s growth into a mature man, and its use in 2:21, where the dwelling place of God, called an οἰκοδομή, “grows” (αὔξει, auxei) as Jews and Gentiles are tightly “joined together” (συναρμολογουμένη, synarmologoumenē) to form it. Here Christ is the head and therefore the source of this unity and growth, just as in 2:20–22 he is architecturally the most important stone in the οἰκοδομή, both guiding its construction and crowning its completion.

This growth, whether of body or building, takes place ἐν ἀγάπῃ (en agapē, in love; cf. v. 15). Only by “bearing with each other in love” will the body or building be able to maintain both its unity (4:2–3) and the integrity of its witness to the gospel truth (4:15).

Second, the various connecting parts of the body are the means through which this growth in unity continually takes place. The body, Paul says, is “being joined [συναρμολογούμενον, synarmologoumenon] and held together [συμβιβαζόμενον, symbibazomenon].” The term συναρμολογούμενον is a repetition of συναρμολογουμένη from the figure of the growing, united temple of Jewish and Gentile believers in 2:21. It recalls the image of a building held together by tightly fitted joints (see the comments on 2:21). The verb συμβιβάζω (symbibazō) clearly means “hold together” in this context, as it does in Col. 2:19, but this is not the most common use of the term. It more frequently appears in political contexts where warring parties “reconcile” their differences (e.g., Herodotus, Hist. 1.74; Thucydides, Pel. War 2.29.6; Plato, Prot. 337e; LSJ 1675; BDAG 956), and Paul may have intended for it to carry those overtones here also.

As we have just seen, Christ, the head, is the ultimate source of the body’s unity, but Paul also says that this unity comes διὰ πάσης ἁφῆς τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας (dia pasēs haphēs tēs epichorēgias, through every assisting connection).[42] The meaning of the term ἁφή (haphē) is unclear and has been the subject of extensive discussion.[43] The common element of the term’s many and varied meanings is the concept of touch or contact (LSJ 288; Hoehner 2002: 573; cf. Abbott 1897: 126; Best 1998: 411), but in the present context, where the structure of the body is under discussion, it probably has an anatomical meaning (Best 1998: 411). An ancient Greek medical dictionary defines the plural (ἁφάς, haphas) as “ties, from ‘to fasten’” (τὰ ἅμματα παρὰ τὸ ἅψαι, ta hammata para to hapsai; Robinson 1904: 186).[44]

This might lead us to translate the term as “ligaments” or “tendons,” but that translation would probably be too specific. Paul depicts these physical ties as giving the body ἐπιχορηγία (epichorēgia), a term that can mean “assistance” (cf. Phil. 1:19; BDAG 387), and he is probably thinking of any of the body’s lines of connection, whether ligaments, arteries, nerves, muscles, or bones (cf. Best 1998: 411). Thought of as a unit, these “connections” provide a mechanical frame, a network of communication, and a means of conveying substances through the body.[45]

They are not, however, a special class of bodily components, corresponding to the five especially gifted groups of verse 11, who help other believers with their work of ministry and in this way nourish the growing body (pace, e.g., Lincoln 1990: 262–63; Schnackenburg 1991: 189; Muddiman 2001: 209). Instead, Paul pictures “every connection” in the body as performing its work of assistance “according to the activity in the measure of each single part” (κατ᾿ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους, kat’ energeian en metrō henos hekastou merous). This recalls the language of 4:7, where Christ gave grace to “each” (ἑκάστῳ, hekastō) believer “according to” (κατά, kata) a certain “measure” (μέτρον, metron), and so it is unlikely that this language now implies the “activity” of only certain special groups within the body. Paul defines “every connection” as “each single part” of the body and uses the body figure to say what he had said at the beginning of the section: Christ measures out grace to each Christian in a way that is appropriate for that Christian’s role in building up the body (vv. 7, 12).

Paul therefore ends the section as it began, with a reference to Christ’s gift of power to every believer in a portion equal to that believer’s role in building up Christ’s body. The Christ who gives these gifts, we are reminded, is the Christ who has conquered all the evil forces of the universe, wherever they are located. He is, therefore, powerful enough to equip the church to keep false teaching at bay, maintain its unity, and reach its destiny of full union with him.

Summary

In 4:7–16 Paul demonstrates that the same power made available to him to fulfill the important responsibility that God has given him to preach the gospel to the Gentiles has also been given to every individual within the church to work for the church’s unity and maturity. Christ has attained victory over the cosmic enemies of God and his people, and now, in a way that is consistent with the picture of God’s victory in Ps. 68, Christ is distributing the spoils of that victory to his people. He has given every believer a role in supporting the church’s growth. Some engage in apostolic activity, others in prophesying, others in evangelizing, others in shepherding, and still others in teaching. The purpose of all this activity is to equip God’s people to build up the church. The ultimate goal of the church’s construction and growth is its unified commitment to doctrinal truth and to the experience of the knowledge of Christ. The more mature the church becomes, the more effective it will be at refuting false teaching and maturing into the body of Christ. For this to happen, each connection within the body must lovingly contribute to the body’s growth.



Additional Notes

4:8. A number of witnesses have καί before ἔδωκεν (e.g., אi2, B, C*, 3, D2, Ψ, 1739, 1881, most Byzantine manuscripts). The καί smooths out the quotation, and this at first seems decisive against it. Yet it also introduces a difference between the quotation and Ps. 67:19 LXX, which does not have the καί (Ellicott 1859: 84). Would a scribe be more likely to make the Greek easier or to conform the text to the LXX? A number of editors (von Soden, Vogels, Bover; see NA27, 764; cf. Abbott 1897: 114) have opted to include the καί, apparently deciding that the pressure to harmonize the quotation to the LXX prompted a scribe somewhere to drop it. The evidence for omitting it, however, is both ancient and geographically diverse (e.g., 𝔓46, א, A, C2, D*, F, G, 33), indicating that it probably did not stand in the original text.

4:9. Some ancient witnesses to the text (e.g., אi2, B, C3, Ψ, most Byzantine manuscripts) read πρῶτον after κατέβη. If this is the correct reading, then an ambiguity in the text is clarified. Without πρῶτον the timing of Christ’s descent is unclear, especially since the quotation mentions only an ascent. The quotation and the interpretation of it might be understood to imply that the ascent from earth to heaven came first and was followed by a descent from heaven back to earth. This pattern would correspond to the legendary visit of several great figures in antiquity to heaven and their subsequent return (e.g., Enoch, Abraham, Moses). With the πρῶτον, however, there can be no doubt that the descent came “first” and was followed by an ascent. The descent, then, could either be from heaven to the earth or from earth to Hades, the regions under the earth. The ascent would, in either case, still be an ascent to heaven.

A copyist might naturally try to bring some clarity to such a difficult text, but it is hard to imagine a motive for omitting an original πρῶτον (Best 1998: 383; Hoehner 2002: 531n3). The ancient and geographically diverse witnesses to the text without πρῶτον (e.g, 𝔓46, א*, A, C*, D, F, G, 082, 6, 33, 81, 1739, 1881) make it virtually certain that it did not appear in the original.

The evidence of the witnesses for (e.g., א, B, C, D2, I, Ψ, most Byzantine manuscripts) and against (e.g., 𝔓46, D*, F, G) reading μέρη after κατώτερα is more evenly divided. The witnesses that have μέρη are ancient and include representatives of the Alexandrian and Byzantine traditions (Hoehner 2002: 533n3). The witnesses that omit the word, however, include early representatives of both the Alexandrian and Western traditions (𝔓46 and D*). Once again, scribal habits must decide the matter: it is difficult to imagine a scribe omitting the word if it were present, but fairly easy to see a scribe making the text more explicit by adding it.

4:11. Two relatively minor points of grammar in this verse have occasioned discussion. First, according to Schnackenburg (1991: 180–181), the μὲν . . . δὲ . . . δὲ . . . δέ construction sets up a contrast between the apostles on one hand (μέν) and the rest of the list on the other hand (δέ). This understanding of the grammar is consistent with Schnackenburg’s exegesis of 3:5, where he argues that in the phrase τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις (to his holy apostles, and prophets) the apostles are set apart from the prophets by the terms ἁγίοις and αὐτοῦ. From the viewpoint of the author of Ephesians, he says, the apostles’ connection with the historical Jesus set them apart from all other early Christian leaders (Schnackenburg 1991: 133–34).

This understanding of the syntax of 3:5 is plausible (see the comments on 3:5), but it is not likely that 4:11 sets up a similar contrast. The μὲν . . . δὲ . . . δέ construction was a normal way of listing discrete items in Hellenistic Greek, with no clear intention of expressing a contrast between the first item in the list and the items that follow it. Justin, Dial. 39.2, is especially instructive, since the subject (receiving gifts from God) is similar to that of Eph. 4:11 but no clear literary relationship exists between the two texts: ὁ μὲν γὰρ λαμβάνει συνέσεως πνεῦμα, ὁ δὲ βουλῆς, ὁ δὲ ἰσχύος, ὁ δὲ ἰάσεως, ὁ δὲ προγνώσεως, ὁ δὲ διδασκαλίας, ὁ δὲ φόβου θεοῦ (For one receives a spirit of understanding, another of counsel, another of strength, another of healing, another of foreknowledge, another of teaching, and another of the fear of God [my trans.]; cf. Lucian, Hermot. 66; Justin, Dial. 35.6; and especially 39.2; Matt. 13:8, 23; BDAG 630). There is certainly no contrast between the first item in this list and any of the others. The same is true of Eph. 4:11.

Second, interpreters have understood the articles that accompany the particles μὲν . . . δὲ . . . δὲ . . . δέ in Eph. 4:11 in two different ways. According to one reading, they should be taken as attributive modifiers of their nouns, and each noun should then be taken as a straightforward direct object of the verb ἔδωκεν (edōken, he gave). The resulting translation is “He himself gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers” (e.g., Merklein 1973: 73–75; Lincoln 1990: 249).

According to the other reading, the articles function with their particles as pronouns. This is a common occurrence in the NT and is well illustrated in the quotation from Justin above. If the articles in Eph. 4:11 are understood in this sense, then each gift is linked to its article-particle combination with an understood verb of being, and each gift forms the predicate of the resulting statement. This seems complex, but it is perfectly intelligible Greek and would yield the translation “He himself gave some to be apostles, others to be prophets, others to be evangelists, and others to be shepherds and teachers” (BDAG 686; Muddiman 2001: 198n6; Hoehner 2002: 538).

What difference does it make? If the first way of taking the articles is correct, then the emphasis falls on certain people insofar as they hold particular positions; if the second way of taking the articles is correct, the emphasis falls on the gifts that these people are given and therefore on the activities they perform. The first option places the accent on the role certain people play whereas the second option places the accent on the work a particular gift allows certain people to perform.

The second option (“He himself gave some to be apostles, others to be prophets, others to be evangelists, and others to be shepherds and teachers”) is probably correct for two reasons. First, if the alternative reading were correct, there would be no indirect object for the verb ἔδωκεν (he gave), and the reader would be left with a sense of incompleteness: he gave apostles and prophets and so forth, but to whom did he give them (Muddiman 2001: 198n6)? Second, in the broader context of verse 11, the emphasis falls on the activities that gifted individuals perform rather than on the people themselves. Although interpreters dispute whether the five groups in verse 11 or all “the saints” perform “the work of ministry” and building up the body in verse 12, the most probable interpretation of this verse sees it as a reference to the work of all believers. If this is correct, the emphasis of verses 11–12 falls on the activities gifted individuals perform rather than on the “offices” they hold.





VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)


IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

In a rhetorical move that by now has become characteristic of Ephesians (cf. 2:5a; 3:14), in 4:17 Paul signals a return to the subject he has left behind in 4:1–3. In that passage, he started to describe in practical terms what it means for the church to grow into the unity that the death of Christ on the cross has achieved for it, according to 2:11–22. It means walking in humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with each other in love, and zealously maintaining the oneness that, according to 2:22, God’s Spirit has given them with each other. The notion of God’s Spirit as the source for the unity of God’s people has then led to a rhythmic set of affirmations of the unity of God (4:4–6) and from there into a description of the gifts that Christ has given the church to equip it to arrive at the unity and maturity that would be its destiny (4:7–16). With the phrase “this therefore I say and charge you in the Lord . . .” in 4:17, Paul begins a return to the practical matters he intended to discuss before the digressions of 4:4–6 and 4:7–16.

The movement into these practical matters is slow. In an opening section, Paul first lays a theological foundation by reminding his readers again of their conversion (4:17–24; cf. 2:1–10, 11–22). Here, however, the focus is not on what God has done for them, as in 2:1–10, or on their unity with each other across ethnic lines, as in 2:11–22, but on the practical, day-to-day ramifications of their movement from futility, darkness, estrangement from God, dullness, and despair to the experience of constant spiritual renewal and re-creation in the image of God (4:24; cf. 2:10, 15).

This opening section (4:17–24) can be divided into two parts. First, Paul exhorts his readers no longer to “walk” in the way that used to characterize their lives as unbelieving Gentiles, and then he provides a motivation for this exhortation by describing in bleak terms the existence of those who continue to live this way (4:17–19; cf. 2:1–3). Second, he reminds his readers of the traditional ethical instruction that he assumes they received after they believed the gospel (4:20–24). He describes the change in behavior that their conversion has entailed with a metaphor for conversion in use in ancient philosophical and religious circles, a metaphor of taking off one set of clothing and replacing it with a new set.[1] He couples this imagery with a second metaphor, which speaks of the change from existence as an old human being to existence as a new human being. At the end of the section, he identifies “the new human being” his readers have become as “created after the pattern of God” (ὁ καινὸς ἄνθρωπος ὁ κατὰ θεὸν κτισθείς, ho kainos anthrōpos ho kata theon ktistheis; 4:24), an allusion to Gen. 1:26.﻿[2]

In 4:25–5:2 Paul is now finally ready to give the concrete ethical instruction he seems to have been preparing for since 4:1–3. The διό (dio, therefore) with which the section begins in 4:25 shows that he understands the exhortations that follow to be illustrations of what it means to live the new life he has just described, particularly life as a human being newly created in God’s image. It seems reasonable to think of these exhortations as reminders of the traditional ethical teaching he hopes (εἴ γε, ei ge, as I assume; v. 21) his readers have received. A series of seven exhortations ensues, covering the following:

lying (v. 25)

anger (vv. 26–27)

stealing (v. 28)

unedifying speech (v. 29)

grieving the Holy Spirit (v. 30)

abusive speech (vv. 31–32)

sacrificial love in imitation of God and Christ (5:1–2).[3]



The place of the final set of exhortations (5:1–2) in the discourse is not clear. Some interpreters take these exhortations as the beginning of a new major division. Unlike the preceding admonitions in 4:25–32, the admonition in 5:1–2 contains no prohibition but is entirely positive (Barth 1974: 555). Like 4:1 and 4:17, verses that begin new major sections of the discourse, this set of exhortations contains both an οὖν (oun, therefore) and a form of the verb περιπατέω (peripateō, walk; Hoehner 2002: 643).

Others see 5:1–2 as the continuation and conclusion of the preceding exhortations. This section repeats the term γίνεσθε (ginesthe, be) from 4:32 and illustrates, with a reference to Christ’s death, the costly nature of the forgiveness of God and therefore the quality of the forgiveness that believers should demonstrate toward each other (e.g., Schnackenburg 1991: 204; O’Brien 1999: 352).

A third approach, however, is probably best. Paul wanted this final set of admonitions to provide a fitting conclusion to the whole section by bringing his ethical advice full circle and so back to the theme of the imitation of God that prompted it (5:1; cf. 4:24).





IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

A. No Longer Walk as “Gentiles” but as a New Human Being (4:17–24)

B. Living as Human Beings Newly Created in God’s Image (4:25–5:2)


A. No Longer Walk as “Gentiles” but as a New Human Being (4:17–24)

Perhaps it is the picture of the church’s destiny as the mature, closely knit, and harmoniously functioning body of Christ in 4:16 that prompted Paul to return to the practical admonitions from which he began to digress in 4:4. In any case, in 4:17 he returns to the solemn, exhortatory language of 4:1 and begins in earnest his practical instruction about how his audience can maintain the oneness that the Spirit has given them according to 4:3.

The first section of this instruction (4:17–24) clarifies for Paul’s audience that their new existence must stand in sharp contrast to the existence of those who stand outside the boundaries of God’s people. Paul begins with the negative, urging his readers no longer to walk as the “Gentiles” walk, and then describes Gentile behavior and existence with four clauses (4:17–19). Their conduct originates in a “futile” way of thinking; their understanding is darkened; because of their ignorance and hard-heartedness, they are estranged from the life that God promises; and in their despondency they have given themselves up to behavior so crazed by greed that it has become antisocial.

It is possible to read this description as a blunt claim that unbelievers are simply foolish, stubborn, utterly selfish, and debauched. To read the text this way, however, is to fail to appreciate the subtlety of Paul’s language. Paul probably linked the futility of the Gentiles’ way of thinking to their failure to worship the true God. Similarly, the darkness of their understanding is related to their existence under the influence of “the world-rulers of this darkness” (6:12; cf. 2:2) or, as Paul put it to the Corinthians, “the demons” to whom Gentiles sacrifice when they worship idols (1 Cor. 10:20). Their ignorance and hard-heartedness are certainly culpable, but they also are pitiable. They are suffering, but they are unaware of why they suffer, and their hopelessness has left them with nothing to live for but their greed. Their greed has, in turn, produced in them all kinds of bizarre behavior.

To this horrific description of the Gentile worldview and the behavior to which it has led, Paul contrasts the worldview and behavior of his readers, assuming that they have actually both entered into a relationship with Christ and received sound instruction in his teaching (4:20–24). The idea that the transformation of their behavior requires a relationship with the living Jesus emerges from the syntactical oddity of following verbs of learning and hearing not with direct objects that describe the content of what was learned and heard but with references to Jesus himself as the object of the learning and hearing. Paul assumes that his audience has “learned Christ” and “heard him.” Their instruction in the foundational elements of the faith, moreover, has come to them “in him.”

Paul summarizes this instruction in three steps. The first and last of these steps make use of a common ancient metaphor for personal transformation: taking off and putting on clothing.

First, if his readers have received sound teaching, they learned to put off the old human being, whose way of living was characterized by continual corruption. That old way of life could result only in personal disintegration, the kind of existence Paul has just described in 4:19—an existence that is guided by demons, hopeless, and so focused on greed that it leads to bizarre and antisocial behavior. It is also behavior that, in the end, is consumed by the wrath of God.

Second, they have learned to be continually renewed in mind. This, too, stands in contrast to the Gentile way of life described in 4:17–20, where the misguided thinking of the Gentiles has left them in darkness.

Third, they have been taught to put on the new human being, created after the pattern of God. Just as in 2:10 and 2:15, the allusion to God’s creation of Adam, the first human being, is clear (cf. Gen. 1:26). Paul’s readers have been newly created in God’s image and therefore in the “righteousness and holiness” that characterize him. Paul’s point is that his readers’ behavior should reflect this new reality. They have been newly created in the image of a righteous and holy God. They too should be righteous and holy.



Exegesis and Exposition

17aTherefore I say and charge [you] in the Lord 17bthat you should no longer walk as the Gentiles walk in the futility of their mind 18because they are darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them because of the hardness of their heart, 19who, ⌜because they have become despondent⌝, have given themselves over to unrestrained debauchery, which results in greedily doing all kinds of uncleanness.

20But you—not so did you learn Christ! 21—If, as I assume, you heard and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus, 22to put off the old human being with respect to your former manner of life that was continually being corrupted because of the cravings of deceit, 23to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, 24and to put on the new human being, created after the pattern of God in the righteousness and holiness of the truth.

[4:17a] With a brief introductory statement, Paul now returns to the moral exhortation from which he had wandered away after 4:1–3, and he signals this return by recalling the language of 4:1. He resumes the first-person singular of that verse, repeats the phrase ἐν κυρίῳ (en kyriō, in the Lord), uses μαρτύρομαι (martyromai, I charge [you]), which is a synonym of παρακαλῶ (parakalō, I encourage [you]) in 4:1 (cf. 1 Thess. 2:12), and repeats the combination of οὖν (oun, therefore) with περιπατέω (peripateō, walk).

The τοῦτο (touto, this) points forward to the moral exhortation he is about to give (cf. 5:5; 6:22), and the emphasis in this introductory statement falls on the solemnity of what will follow. Paul communicates this solemnity in three ways.

First, he uses redundancy. He does not merely “say” what his readers should do; he also “charges” them to behave in a certain way.

Second, he shifts back to the first-person singular and uses the phrase ἐν κυρίῳ. This recalls the language of 4:1 and before that of 3:1, with their connotations of authority. Paul, the prisoner “in the Lord” (4:1) and “of Christ” (3:1)—one of the holy apostles (3:5), who form the foundation of the church (2:20)—issues the instructions that follow.

Third, he uses the term μαρτύρομαι to describe his charge to them. This is a solemn term, often used to put people on notice that they must carry out a particular behavior or serious consequences will follow (Thucydides, Pel. War 8.53.2; Polybius, Hist. 13.8.1; Jdt. 7:28; Josephus, Ant. 10.10; cf. Gal. 5:3).[1] The moral exhortation here is not merely advice that Paul’s readers can take or leave at their discretion but is critical instruction for becoming the human beings and the community that God intends for them to be.

[4:17b–19] Paul begins his exhortation by describing how his readers should not “walk.” Although there is a physical sense in which they are still Gentiles—they are not circumcised (2:11; 3:1)—they have nevertheless been created anew by their union with the crucified, risen, exalted Christ (2:5–6, 10, 15), and so there is another sense in which they are no longer Gentiles (cf. 1 Cor. 5:1; 12:2). Paul speaks of this sense when he now says they should no longer walk as Gentiles.

Gentiles who have not experienced union with Christ have four problems that Paul describes in language typical of Hellenistic Jewish descriptions of Gentile vices.

First, they walk ἐν ματαιότητι τοῦ νοὸς αὐτῶν (en mataiotēti tou noos autōn, in the futility of their mind). The adjective μάταιος (mataios, “idle, empty, fruitless, useless, powerless, lacking truth” [BDAG 621]) was sometimes used as a plural substantive in the literature of Hellenistic Judaism to refer to Gentile idols (Jer. 2:5; 8:19 LXX), and so Gentiles, who worshiped these dumb images, were naturally thought of as ματαιόφρονες (mataiophrones), “empty minded” (3 Macc. 6:11). They were “ignorant of God, . . . foolish by nature; and they were unable from the good things that are seen to know the one who exists” (Wis. 13:1 NRSV), or as Paul puts it in Rom. 1:21, “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but they became futile in their thoughts [ἐματαιώθησαν ἐν τοῖς διαλογισμοῖς, emataiōthēsan en tois dialogismois], and their senseless [ἀσύνετος, asynetos] heart was darkened [ἐσκοτίσθη, eskotisthē].” The worshipful acknowledgment of the one God is foundational to all useful knowledge. Without this foundation, Gentile knowledge about how to live one’s life is deeply flawed.

Second, they are ἐσκοτωμένοι τῇ διανοίᾳ ὄντες (eskotōmenoi tē dianoia ontes, darkened in understanding).[2] The language is close to Rom. 1:21, and just as in that text, the two ideas of a useless mind and a darkened understanding should not be interpreted separately: they are mutually reinforcing. Formally, ὄντες is an adverbial participle of cause, describing why the Gentiles conduct their lives according to a futile way of thinking. They do this “because,” as far as their understanding is concerned, they exist in darkness.

Later Paul will say that his readers, in their former existence, “were . . . darkness [σκότος, skotos]” (5:8) and that they should avoid partnering with “the unfruitful works of darkness [σκότος]” (5:11). That way of life is closely allied with the evil spirits that continue to have power in the present age of “darkness” (6:12; cf. 2:2–3).

The picture is of an existence that is aimless because it is ignorant of the truth and is kept in this condition by powerful spiritual forces.[3] It meshes with 2:2–3 and is probably intended to remind the readers of that description of their existence prior to experiencing the mercy, love, and grace of God (2:4–9), and prior to their own re-creation for the purpose of “walking” in good works (2:10; Heil 2007a: 189).[4]

Third, they are ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ θεοῦ (apēllotriōmenoi tēs zōēs tou theou, alienated from the life of God).[5] The perfect participle ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι must have recalled for Paul’s readers the use of precisely the same word in the same form in 2:12, where it referred to their plight before they believed the gospel: they were “alienated” from citizenship in Israel, from the covenant promises of Israel’s Scriptures, and from the God who made those promises. God’s most important covenant promise to Israel was that he would give them “life” (Deut. 30:15–20). Both Jews and Gentiles had become estranged from the life that God promised (2:2–3; cf. Gal. 2:15–16; Rom. 1:18–3:20), but here Paul’s focus is on the Gentiles.

Paul describes the cause of this alienation in two prepositional phrases that stand parallel to each other and are probably meant to interpret each other. Their estrangement from God, he says, is because of the ἄγνοια (agnoia, ignorance) that exists within them. This term is associated with sin in Jewish literature of the Second Temple period (e.g., 1 Esd. 8:72 LXX [8:75 Eng.]; 9:20; Wis. 14:22; Sir. 23:3), sometimes with the connotation that the sin is less culpable because it was committed in ignorance (Pss. Sol. 13.7; 18.4; cf. Lev. 5:18). The word appears twice in the NT with this connotation (Acts 3:17; 17:30).[6] Here Paul is not trying to play down the complicity of the Gentiles in their rebellion against God (something he clearly affirms in 4:19; 2:2; and 5:6), but his emphasis does lie less on the willfulness of their disobedience than on their lack of understanding and aimlessness.

Paul next repeats the same thought in different terms. Ἡ πώρωσις τῆς καρδίας (hē pōrōsis tēs kardias, hardness of heart) has produced their estrangement from God. In the NT, “hardness of heart” can refer to a stubbornly negative response to Jesus, such as when the Pharisees plot Jesus’s murder after he heals on the Sabbath (Mark 3:5), or to God’s action of hardening the heart of those who have refused to believe in Jesus (John 12:40; cf. Rom. 11:25). The image can also be used of Jesus’s disciples, however, with a slightly different nuance. Their hardness of heart is connected with a more pitiable failure to understand, a dullness that leaves them fearful and clueless about the true state of affairs (Mark 6:52; 8:17). There is no doubt that the disciples’ lack of understanding is an indictment—it places them with “those on the outside” (Mark 4:11), but their hardness of heart is still not precisely like the hardness of the Pharisees’ heart.[7] This “numbness” is Paul’s emphasis here (Theodoret: ἀναλγησία, analgēsia [PG 82:537]; Abbott 1897: 131; Robinson 1904: 273). Unbelieving Gentiles are people who do not understand God or the world as it truly is.[8] Their life, as John of Damascus put it, “has neither finish line nor goal, but is carried out in futility” (PG 95:844, my trans.).[9]

Fourth, Paul confirms the statement he has just made with a further, lengthier explanation.[10] Gentiles, “because they have become despondent [ἀπηλγηκότες, apēlgēkotes], have given themselves over [ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν, heautous paredōkan] to unrestrained debauchery [ἀσελγείᾳ, aselgeia].” The participle ἀπηλγηκότες gives the cause of the Gentiles’ abandonment of moral restraint. This is the only occurrence of the term ἀπαλγέω (apalgeō, become despondent) in the NT, and it is not common in classical literature. It can mean to abandon (ἀπό, apo) one’s personal sense of pain (ἀλγεινός, algeinos) in a noble act of self-discipline for the common good (Thucydides, Pel. War 2.61.4; Plutarch, Ag. Cleom. 22.3). It can also mean, although rarely, to act without a conscience, as a historian does when he knows full well that some fantastic rumor is false and useless but incorporates it into his account anyway (Polybius, Hist. 16.2). This is the way most commentators take it here in Ephesians, and since the previous verse has referred to the “dullness” or “numbness” of Gentiles, this understanding of the term may be correct.

Most often, however, the term refers to despondency so severe that one has abandoned, or nearly abandoned, hope (Polybius, Hist. 1.35.5 [cf. 1.31.8]; 1.58.9). Such desperation could, in turn, lead to violent public policy (Polybius, Hist. 9.40.4) or suicide (Philo, Rewards 135). Robinson (1904: 189) comments perceptively that desperation and reckless living “are moods which stand not far apart,” and it seems likely that both “moods” overlap in Paul’s use of the term here. The early interpreter of the text who first replaced ἀπηλγηκότες with ἀπηλπικότες (apēlpikotes, because they despaired) failed to copy the text correctly (see the additional note) but correctly understood Paul’s meaning. The stupor and aimlessness with which Gentiles make their way through life leads them to despair, and in their despair, they give themselves over to “unrestrained debauchery” (ἀσέλγεια, aselgeia).

In Hellenistic Jewish texts, ἀσέλγεια refers to twisted behavior (e.g., Wis. 14:26; Josephus, Ant. 8.252), often of a sexual nature and in defiance of God (e.g., 3 Macc. 2:25–26 [cf. 1:10–12, 26]; Josephus, Ant. 8.318). There is an open, shameless element to ἀσέλγεια (Josephus, Ant. 20.112; cf. 108). Those who engage in it indulge a selfish desire to assert one’s absolute right (αὐτεξούσιος, autexousios) to pleasure, no matter what anyone else might think of it, and in flagrant rebellion against the law (Josephus, Ant. 4.151; cf. 145–49). Paul drives this element of the word home with his comment that the ἀσέλγεια of the Gentiles “results in greedily doing all kinds of [πάσης, pasēs] uncleanness.”[11] When ἀσέλγεια appears in vice lists elsewhere in Paul’s letters, he always associates it with other words that refer to unrestrained sexual activity (Gal. 5:19; 2 Cor. 12:21; Rom. 13:13), and that is probably the meaning here.

The Gentiles, Paul says, have “handed themselves over” (ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν) to this sort of behavior. The picture is of people so unhappy that they have delivered themselves up to the destructive forces of their own, unrestrained appetites.

[4:20–21] The behavior of Paul’s readers must bear no resemblance to the way of life he has just described. The ὑμεῖς (hymeis, you) is first in the sentence for emphasis, and the δὲ οὐχ οὕτως (de ouch houtōs, but not so) strikes a strong note of contrast difficult to reproduce in English. The translation, “but you—not so did you learn Christ!” although hardly elegant, perhaps communicates the rhetorical emphasis. The expression “learn Christ” is unusual since the verb μανθάνω (manthanō, learn) does not typically have a person as its object. The construction is not, however, as rare as some commentators imply (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 99–100; Robinson 1904: 190; Abbott 1897: 134; Lincoln 1990: 279; Schnackenburg 1991: 199). Philosophical writers of roughly Paul’s time could apparently speak of “learning God” in the sense not merely of learning about him but in the more relational sense of “renewing” one’s “kinship with him” (“Chion of Heraclea,” Ep. 16.8; cf. 16.6; Tatian, Or. graec. 9.2).[12] This is similar to the way Paul uses the phrase here. Paul conceives of Christ as a living person, seated with God in the heavenly places (1:20), and so he thinks of those who believe in Christ as having a relationship with him: they are seated with him in the heavenly places (2:6), and Christ lives in their hearts (3:17). When they first believed the gospel (1:13) and then continued to mature in their faith (4:13), they certainly learned about Christ and his teachings, but they have also developed a relationship with him as a living person (cf. Gal. 2:20; Phil. 1:21; 3:8–10; 4:13; Col. 3:3; Best 1997a: 141).

Just as in 3:2 (see the comments there), the γέ (ge) adds emphasis to the εἰ, and together the two words communicate an assumption—something Paul knows to be true, but not on the basis of firsthand experience: “if, as I assume, you heard him.” Much had changed in the more than seven years since Paul was last in Ephesus, and even when he was there, some of the Christians in the city had only a loose connection with him (Acts 18:24–28; cf. Trebilco 2004: 115–27). There is no irony here (pace Muddiman 2001: 216–17). Rather, the slight note of uncertainty in the phrase εἰ γέ probably reflects Paul’s knowledge that false understandings of the Christian tradition were abroad (4:14; Col. 2:8–23). It is just possible, he hints, that some of his readers have not heard the Christian message “as the truth is in Jesus.”

The expression αὐτὸν ἠκούσατε (auton ēkousate, you heard him) is almost as unusual as “you learned Christ” in verse 20 (Best 1998: 427; pace Lincoln 1990: 280; Hoehner 2002: 595).[13] As with that expression, the implication is that Christ is alive and that when one hears the gospel preached, as Paul assumes his readers have (1:13), one is put in touch with a living person (Best 1997a: 141). The Paul of the undisputed letters can speak in the same way of announcing Christ as good news (Gal. 1:16; Phil. 1:16–17), of preaching Christ (1 Cor. 1:23; 15:12), and of gaining Christ (Phil. 3:8).[14]

The relational emphasis continues in the next phrase, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐδιδάχθητε (kai en autō edidachthēte, and you were taught in him). Paul assumes that after his readers heard and believed the gospel, they continued to learn more about the Christian tradition. He not only gives this kind of instruction to the Christian communities he has established through his own preaching (1 Thess. 4:2, 11; 2 Thess. 2:15; 3:6; 1 Cor. 11:2); he also assumes that it is a standard feature of Christianity generally (Rom. 6:17). The qualifying phrase ἐν αὐτῷ (en autō, in him) reveals, however, that once again Paul is referring to more than learning information about Christ. The teaching has taken place in the sphere marked out by the living Christ and thus in a way that is possible only for those who have a relationship with him (Best 1997a: 141).

Paul’s next phrase is puzzling for several reasons. First, it is unclear how he uses the adverb καθώς (kathōs). Does it introduce the reason why Paul’s readers learned Christ (Best 1998: 414, 428–29)? Or does it tell the manner in which they were taught (Ellicott 1859: 100; Eadie 1883: 337; cf. La Potterie 1963: 47–48; Hoehner 2002: 598)? This second way of construing the grammar is the simplest since it attaches καθώς to the immediately preceding ἐδιδάχθητε (edidachthēte, you were taught) rather than to the more remote verb ἐμάθετε (emathete, you learned).[15]

Second, without the article in front of ἀλήθεια (alētheia, truth) the meaning of ἐστιν ἀλήθεια ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ (estin alētheia en tō Iēsou, truth is in Jesus) is unclear. Should we use a preparatory “there” to translate ἐστιν (“there is truth in Jesus”; Westcott 1906: 70–71)? Should we take “Christ” from the end of verse 20 as the subject of ἐστιν (“he [Christ] is the truth in Jesus”; cf. F. J. A. Hort [Westcott 1906: 70–71]; Abbott 1897: 136; La Potterie 1963: 48)?[16] Or is ἀλήθεια the subject, despite its lack of an article to indicate this clearly (“the truth is in Jesus”; Lincoln 1990: 281)? The last solution makes the most sense of the (admittedly unusual) syntax and at the same time yields the most intelligible meaning. Abstract nouns, even when they are definite, often omit the article (BDF §258; Zerwick 1963: 57 §179; Lincoln 1990: 281; Wallace 1996: 249), and the simple aphorism “the truth is in Jesus” is more readily understandable than the other options.[17]

Third, it is not clear why Paul has switched from the designation “Christ” to the name “Jesus.” This might simply be a stylistic variation with little or no significance (Lincoln 1990: 281–82), but it is the only place in the letter where the name “Jesus” is used alone. Most commentators are probably correct, then, in thinking that Paul places special emphasis here on the foundation of Christian teaching, particularly its ethics, in the teaching and conduct of Jesus during his earthly ministry (cf. 4:32; 5:2; Aletti 2001: 236).

If we put these three exegetical decisions together, then in this final clause of 4:20–21, Paul describes to his readers the manner in which he assumes they have been taught the Christian tradition. He thinks and hopes that their teaching has been consistent with the truth as it is found in the life and teaching of Jesus of Nazareth. Paul is aware of other, erroneous forms of teaching about Jesus (4:14–15; cf. Col. 2:8–23), but he trusts that the foundation of his readers’ faith was laid by the apostles with their connection to the historical Jesus. Even if most of his readers have heard the gospel and were encouraged in the faith through the work of prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers (2:20; 3:5; 4:11), what they heard and believed, he assumes, was nevertheless the apostolic “word of truth” (1:13).

In 4:20–21, then, Paul begins to set Christian teaching in contrast to a Gentile worldview. To guide their lives, Christians have both a relationship with the living Christ and concrete instruction, derived from the life and teaching of Jesus of Nazareth. The shape of their lives, thus guided, stands utterly apart from the hopeless and socially destructive behavior of their unbelieving Gentile neighbors.

[4:22] In 4:22–24 Paul uses three infinitives to specify what his readers were taught (ἀποθέσθαι, apothesthai, put off [v. 22]; ἀνανεοῦσθαι, ananeousthai, being renewed [v. 23]; ἐνδύσασθαι, endysasthai, put on [v. 24]). From the forms of these verbs, it is not possible to tell whether the original instruction consisted of statements (e.g., Eadie 1883: 338; Hoehner 2002: 600–602) or commands (e.g., Bruce 1984: 357–58; Best 1998: 430–31; Darko 2008: 39).[18] Were Paul’s readers taught that the transformation of their lives has already happened or that it should happen?

The close parallels to Paul’s language in Romans and Colossians can help with this question. In Rom. 6:6 Paul states that “our old human being has been crucified together with [Christ]” (cf. Rom. 6:8; 8:8, 10; Gal. 2:19; 3:27; 6:14), and in Rom. 13:12 and 14 he commands his readers to “put off” (ἀποθώμεθα, apothōmetha) the works of darkness and to “put on” (ἐνδυσώμεθα, endysōmetha; ἐνδύσασθε, endysasthe) the armor of light and the Lord Jesus Christ. Similarly, in Col. 3:8 Paul commands the Colossian Christians to “put off” (ἀπόθεσθε, apothesthe) a list of vices but then in 3:9 asserts that they “have put off the old human being” (ἀπεκδυσάμενοι, apekdysamenoi). Paul can easily swivel between indicative and imperative statements when he uses this kind of language, but in either case the overall purpose is imperatival. He urges his readers to live in a way that is consistent with their new identity in Christ. Here in Eph. 4:22–24, then, the question of whether indicatives or imperatives lie beneath the infinitives ἀποθέσθαι, ἀνανεοῦσθαι, and ἐνδύσασθαι remains unclear, but the passage has an imperatival intent. Paul assumes that his readers have been taught, in Christ, to “put off” their old way of life, “to be [continually] renewed” in their thinking, and “to put on” a new way of life that matches God’s original design for his human creatures.

First, then, they have learned “to put off . . . the old human being” (ἀποθέσθαι ὑμᾶς . . . τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον, apothesthai hymas . . . ton palaion anthrōpon). As the corresponding expression “put on the new human being” (ἐνδύσασθαι τὸν καινὸν ἄνθρωπον, endysasthai ton kainon anthrōpon) in verse 24 shows, Paul refers to taking off and putting on clothing. Some interpreters have thought that this language reflects an early Christian baptismal ritual in which clothing was removed before baptism and then replaced afterward (e.g., Meeks 1974: 182, 183–85; 1983: 151; Dahl 2000: 427–28; Kim 2004: 96, 175–91; cf. Wedderburn 1987: 339), but this is not likely to be correct. It is true that elsewhere Paul connects the metaphor of putting on (Gal. 3:27) or taking off clothing (Col. 2:11–12) with baptism, but he does not even mention baptism here, and no clear evidence exists for a Christian ritual of undressing before baptism and re-dressing afterward until the third century (Hippolytus, Trad. ap. 21.3, 11, 20). Even when it does finally appear, the ritual involves taking off and putting on the same set of clothes, not putting off old clothes and putting on new ones, and its purpose probably had more to do with allowing the waters of baptism unimpeded contact with the whole person than with any symbolism connected with the clothing itself (Stewart-Sykes 2001: 120).

It is more likely that Paul uses the language of taking off and putting on clothing here in a metaphorical way, much as it is used in the OT (e.g., Job 29:14; 40:10; Pss. 93:1 [92:1 LXX]; 104:1 [103:1 LXX]; 132:9 [131:9 LXX]), Hellenistic Judaism (e.g., Philo, Drunkenness 7, 86; Let. Aris. 124), and Greek philosophy (e.g., Plato, Resp. 5.457a).[19] In these contexts, the metaphor refers to adopting certain qualities such as strength, righteousness, honor, majesty, and virtue, or to “putting off the human being” (ἐκδῦναι τὸν ἄνθρωπον, ekdynai ton anthrōpon) in the sense of working against instinctive human habits.[20] Paul, too, is concerned with ethics, both putting off the old human being that behaves according to “the desires of deceit” (v. 22; cf. v. 25) and putting on the new human being that behaves as its Creator intended, with “the righteousness and holiness of the truth” (v. 24).

Paul, then, assumes his readers have learned “to put off” τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον (ton palaion anthrōpon, the old human being) and that they are to do this κατὰ τὴν προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν (kata tēn proteran anastrophēn, with respect to your former manner of life). The preposition κατά (kata) here means “with respect to, in relation to” (BDAG 513; Ellicott 1859: 101; Abbott 1897: 136), and the phrase itself reveals what the term “old human being” means: it refers to “the manner of life” (ἀναστροφή, anastrophē) that defined the existence of Paul’s readers before they believed the gospel (cf. Gal. 1:13). Paul has described this way of life clearly in 2:1–3 (where he uses the verbal form of the noun ἀναστροφή) and in 4:17–19. Both passages depict an existence characterized by numbness, ignorance, and rebellion against God, of people led to destruction by evil powers and inward rebellions that they are helpless to remedy.

Paul now complements that bleak picture by describing the “old human being” as φθειρόμενον κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀπάτης (phtheiromenon kata tas epithymias tēs apatēs, continually being corrupted because of the cravings of deceit).[21] The term φθειρόμενον (phtheiromenon) is in the present tense and so refers to an ongoing process of ruin. Paul uses the term elsewhere only in his Corinthian correspondence, where it appears five times and refers to the moral corruption of people through deceitful and harmful teaching (1 Cor. 15:33; 2 Cor. 11:3; cf. 2 Cor. 7:2) and once, in a play on the word’s range of meaning, to refer first to the corruption of the church and then to God’s punishment of those responsible for the church’s corruption: “If anyone ruins [φθείρει, phtheirei] the temple of God, God will ruin [φθερεῖ] that person” (1 Cor. 3:17). In other contexts the term can have specifically sexual connotations of corruption through seduction (e.g., Josephus, Ant. 4.252; Rev. 19:2; Justin, 1 Apol. 9.4; BDAG 1054).

The origin of these continually corrupting desires, Paul says, is ἀπάτη (apatē), a word that could mean either “deceit” or “pleasure,” and like φθείρω it often has sexual connotations. Judith, for example, can use it of the “deceit” by which she lured the evil Assyrian general Holofernes to his doom through a promise of sexual pleasure that she never intended to fulfill (Jdt. 9:10, 13; cf. 16:8). The goddess Aphrodite, says Strabo, was called “Deceiver” (Ἀπάτουρον, Apatouron) for much the same reason. She lured a group of attacking giants to their deaths ἐξ ἀπάτης (ex apatēs, by deceit) when she tricked them into allowing her to receive them in a cave one by one. As each giant entered, she handed him over to the god Heracles, who was hidden in the cave and killed each one (Strabo, Geogr. 11.2.10; Spicq, TLNT 1:155).

Ἀπάτη and φθείρω come together in 4 Macc. 18:8. There the pious Jewish mother of the Maccabean martyrs describes herself this way: “No seducer corrupted (ἔφθειρεν, ephtheiren) me on a desert plain, nor did the destroyer, the deceitful (ἀπάτης, apatēs) serpent, defile the purity of my virginity” (NRSV; cf. 2 Cor. 11:3).

Paul would probably have been more specific if sexual sins were his only concern here, but the mechanism of sexual sin illustrates Paul’s point well. False ideas made persuasive by the promise of pleasure lead to destructive behavior. The destruction is both self-inflicted in the present (cf. Eph. 4:19) and eventually results in the eschatological ruin that God will bring “upon the sons of disobedience” (2:2–3; 5:6).[22]

In summary, Paul assumes that his readers have received instruction first about putting off their old way of life in which deceit and desire combined to produce a ruinous existence. The end of that way of life could only be destruction.

[4:23] Second, Paul assumes that his readers have learned to be renewed continually in their thinking. Like φθειρόμενον (phtheiromenon, being corrupted), the verb ἀνανεοῦσθαι (ananeousthai) is in the present tense, referring to an ongoing process. The two processes of continual corruption and continual renewal, then, stand in contrast to each other: Paul’s readers are no longer on a self-destructive and ultimately ruinous path but are experiencing continual renewal (cf. Rom. 12:2).

This renewal takes place τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν (tō pneumati tou noos hymōn). This phrase could mean either “by the Spirit of your mind” and refer to the work of God’s Spirit in the renewal of the believer’s mind,[23] or it could mean “in the spirit of your mind” and refer to the location of the renewal as the inward life of the believer.[24] Out of fourteen uses of the term πνεῦμα (pneuma, spirit) in Ephesians, twelve clearly refer to the Spirit of God and one, just as clearly, refers to an evil spirit (2:2). In other words, in this letter the term tends to refer to a spiritual being, not to a faculty or aspect of human existence.

It would clearly refer to God’s Spirit here if it were not for the genitive qualifier τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν (tou noos hymōn, of your mind). This phrase would be an odd way of saying “within your mind” and is most naturally understood to mean that the spirit belongs to the mind or is identical with the mind (Eadie 1883: 342; Abbott 1897: 137; Lincoln 1990: 287). It is likely, then, that in a way typical of the use of the genitive elsewhere in this letter, the expression is redundant (Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 87; Lincoln 1990: 287), an emphatic way of referring to what Paul calls in 3:16 “the inner human being” (ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος, ho esō anthrōpos) or in 1 Cor. 2:11 “the spirit of the human being, which is in him” and “knows” him.[25]

Having said all this, it is still appropriate to see God’s Spirit “hovering nearby,” as Fee (1994: 712) memorably puts it. Paul speaks of “being renewed,” in the passive voice, and the agent of the passive action is clearly God. God works “through his Spirit in the inner human being” (3:16), and so the inward renewal that Paul describes here is something that the Spirit accomplishes in believers.

[4:24] Third, Paul’s readers have learned to “put on [ἐνδύσασθαι, endysasthai] the new human being.” Paul has described the old human being as “being corrupted because of the cravings of deceit.” Now he describes the new human being, in contrast, as τὸν κατὰ θεὸν κτισθέντα (ton kata theon ktisthenta, created after the pattern of God). This language recalls Gen. 1:26 LXX: “Then God said, ‘Let us make humankind according to our image [κατ᾿ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν, kat’ eikona hēmeteran] and according to likeness [καθ᾿ ὁμοίωσιν, kath’ homoiōsin]’” (NETS). The echo is more explicit in the closely related Col. 3:10 (“And having put on the new human being, renewed in knowledge according to the image [κατ᾿ εἰκόνα, kat’ eikona] of the one who created him”), but since the theme of a new human creation has already risen to prominence in Eph. 2:10, 15, Paul’s audience would not miss it here. The renewal of their minds from the corruption and despair characteristic of the worldview of those in rebellion against God is part of God’s re-creative work of restoring the universe to its original harmony with himself and, internally, with itself. The theme is also present, although less prominently, in the undisputed Pauline letters (Gal. 6:15; 2 Cor. 5:17).

If Paul’s readers are created in God’s image, then, like God, they exist ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ καὶ ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας (en dikaiosynē kai hosiotēti tēs alētheias, in the righteousness and holiness of the truth). The two virtues “righteousness” and “holiness” are often paired in ancient philosophical and religious literature. Sometimes these terms (whether in nominal, adjectival, or adverbial form) are used to describe the divinity or his actions (e.g., Deut. 32:4; Ps. 144:17 LXX [145:17 MT, Eng.]; Pss. Sol. 10.5; Rev. 16:5; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.26.32]; BDAG 728), sometimes to describe the character that people should have (e.g., Plato, Apol. 35d; Crito 54b; Wis. 9:3; Pss. Sol. 15.3; 1 Thess. 2:10; Titus 1:8; Luke 1:75), and occasionally, as here, to say that people should imitate the character of God (Plato, Theaet. 176b; Philo, Flight 63; Wild 1985: 130).

It is possible that Paul intends to distinguish between the two virtues, as, for example, Philo does when he speaks of “holiness [ὁσιότης, hosiotēs] toward God and righteousness [δικαιοσύνη, dikaiosynē] toward people” (Abraham 208; e.g., Eadie 1883: 345; cf. Hoehner 2002: 612). The two qualities could be used together in a more general way, however, simply to mean “virtue” (Plato, Theaet. 176b), and Wild has shown that when Philo distinguishes between the two terms, he carefully lists “holiness” before “justice.” Since the order here in Eph. 4:24 is the reverse, Wild (1985: 134) concludes that the two terms probably “refer simply to ‘virtuous living’ as a whole.”

We might add to this that in 4:24 Paul is still introducing his more specific and concrete ethical instruction. He has not yet started to speak in practical terms of how the believer should live—that will come in the next verse. It is likely, then, that here he intends to speak in a general way of putting on the virtuous qualities that characterize God himself rather than of specific duties to God and neighbor.

Paul qualifies both “righteousness” and “holiness” with τῆς ἀληθείας (tēs alētheias, of the truth). Some interpreters (e.g., Best 1998: 438; Muddiman 2001: 221) take this qualifier as an adjective (“true righteousness and holiness”), but for two reasons this is probably too bland an understanding of the word. First, “righteousness” and “holiness” are self-evidently “true,” and so to explicitly describe them this way seems to add redundancy to an already-redundant phrase. Second, Paul’s previous uses of “truth” as a concept are connected with specifically Christian truth: the gospel and the Jesus whom it proclaims (1:13; 4:15, 21). It seems more likely, then, that τῆς ἀληθείας is a genitive of source (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 288; Hoehner 2002: 613). Just as deceit was the origin of the evil desires that continually corrupt “the old human being” (4:22), so now Paul says that the righteousness and holiness characteristic of the “new human being” originate in the truth about God as it is described in the gospel (1:13; 4:15) and is seen in the Jesus whom the gospel proclaims (4:21).

Summary

In 4:17–24, Paul says that the lives of his readers should reflect the dramatic transformation that has taken place in them at their conversion. They should no longer live in a way that speaks of the confusion, demonic control, and despair that characterize those who are estranged from the life God provides. They should instead live in ways that show their thinking is continually being renewed spiritually and that reveal their re-creation in the image of a God who is righteous and holy.



Additional Note

4:19. Instead of ἀπηλγηκότες, a few manuscripts (e.g., 𝔓99, D, P, 1241), versions (e.g., some Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate, and the Armenian, Ethopic, and Slavic versions), and fathers (e.g., Irenaeus [in Latin translation], Victorinus of Rome, Ambrosiaster, Jerome, Pelagius, Speculum) read ἀπηλπικότες (because they despaired). Two codices (F, G) have the alternative spelling ἀφηλπικότες. Although there is a bit of geographical diversity among these witnesses (D, F, and G are Western; P is Alexandrian), ἀπηλγηκότες has on its side virtually the entire Alexandrian and Byzantine traditions. It is easy to imagine a scribe harmonizing this text with 2:12 by the slight alteration of what was probably an unfamiliar word. There can be little doubt, then, that ἀπηλγηκότες is the right reading.
